speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, August 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde for concurrence in the second report of the standing committee on industrial relations.
Mr. NORMAN J. M. LOCKHART (Lincoln) : Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last night at seven o'clock, at which time there was some slight interruption to deal with the continuity of business in the house, I was speaking about the forty-hour week, and there is reference in the press to-day to certain labour demands across the country in this respect. I said then that I thought it was ill-conceived, and referred to the fact that the 48-hour week provision had been placed on the statute books of Ontario as recently as January 1 of this year. I expressed the opinion that it should have been tried out for at least a period of time before any attempt was made to drop hours of labour down to forty hours per week.
Much criticism has been launched against the so-called ten-cent pattern credited to the provincial board, and approved at least in theory by the present government. Let me
say here that I am just as definitely opposed to rigid patterns such as the 40-hour week as I am to the ten-cent wage pattern which has been criticized, and especially at a time when the country faces a crisis. In my opinion it is ill-conceived 'to try to force the forty-hour week, in the light of many complications which have arisen. If hon. members will bear with me for only a few minutes I shall endeavour to show how this reduction of hours works out, and will illustrate by citing one case which I know is common to many thousands across Canada, in connection with the working out of the 48-hour week. This is not a hypothetical case, but one within my own personal experience.
I have in my files a considerable number of letters from small employers, which I shall not attempt to read. However, the particular instance I have in mind concerns an employer who has from forty to fifty employees. Long before the war this man assisted financially some seven or eight of his employees to get small houses. He lent them small amounts of money, and allowed them to use their-

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I must point out there is so much noise in the chamber that it is disagreeable not only to the hon. member who has the floor, but also to those who want to listen.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the side discussions end, I shall proceed. I was pointing out that I have on my files much evidence to support what I am about to say. Before the war this particular employer, whom I have known for thirty or thirty-five years, had forty or fifty employees on his payroll, and he had assisted at least seven or eight of them in securing small houses. He lent them small amounts of money and did many other things for their assistance. He allowed them to use his trucking equipment in the erection of those houses. Long before this so-called blue-plan for hospital care became known, this man had worked out a scheme under which his employees would contribute a small amount per week, and he matched their contributions dollar for dollar in order to provide social security for them. I could go on at length, setting out the various things he did to help them. The employees were permitted to control the payment of this money. At times when there were hospital emergencies, doctors' bills, the arrival of children in the families, dental care and many other obligations, $25 or $50 was always available through that fund. The fund was set up in trust, and the expenditures were controlled by the employees. The employer did all sorts of things like that. Needless to say the esprit
Industrial Relations

de corps in that plant was good, and, what is more, the employer and his employees were drawn more closely together by these arrangements.
I thought of this when I listened to one hon. member who said, I believe it was in connection with the steel strike at Hamilton, that Mr. Brockington had to introduce the head of the industry to the head of the union. This kind of thing shows the necessity of getting closer together. In the case I have cited the employees were working from 52 to 54 hours per week. The employer called in his men and he said, "From January 1 you will be working only 48 hours a week, but we are going to continue to give you the same take-home pay. This is going to cost us from $8,000 to $10,000, but we will do our best to absorb the added expense." He continued, and I have correspondence to confirm what he said, "Remember we expect your hundred per cent cooperation. We have had to work largely under ceiling prices with the goods we distribute, and the added cost for labour will come out of our profits. Our turnover must be kept up, or our earnings will decrease." That was the conversation about which he has written. He said, "If we work together perhaps it will work out; we ire willing to do our part." He added one filing more which is very significant. He said, 'If our turnover decreases and our earnings are depleted, it will become necessary because of this reduction to 48 hours to put on five or six more men in order to get out the work." It was pointed out that this would mean increased overhead. I think this goes to show the position in which the small employer is placed. The men rallied around the employer and everything went well for a few months. Then this present unrest-this is the part I want to emphasize-started to creep into the ranks of these forty to fifty men, and trouble started. I have a letter yesterday setting out the details. Four or five of the men said that they were going to work only 40 hours a week from now on. There was' a reduction from 52 to 54 hours to 48 hours a week; but what is going to happen when the 40-hour week is put into effect?
Our whole system of employment is being disrupted by these tactics. This employer also writes that his truck drivers have become dissatisfied. An organizer has come in trying to get them into the track drivers' union or something. These drivers have dropped into their old habits of stopping at the beer parlour and taking on a few glasses of beer. This man's overhead is piling up and he writes me that yesterday he posted a notice that as of September 1 there will be a reduction of

five per cent in wages. This is made necessary because earnings have been going down. This is an example of the vicious circle that is created by this sort of thing, and I am convinced that it is illustrative of thousands of similar cases across the country. If these things do not work out it, in the end, will reflect upon the workers themselves. It is high time that an opportunity was given for a general discussion of the whole matter.
I should like to say just a word about law and order. The public are becoming exasperated at the flagrant violations of the laws of our land by all parties concerned. You hear talk of this on the streets and on the trains. Public opinion is demanding some action, and is holding the governing parties responsible for the maintenance of law and order. The most definite criticism falls in the lap of the federal government who are responsible for the setting up of the wartime prices and trade board, the regional war labour boards, the national war labour board and all other government bodies. This is the result of their policy. That is what the people are saying.
I am trying to discuss this thing without rancour or prejudice; I am trying to be fair and present the case as I know it. That is what is being said on the streets. The people say, "If our laws are wrong, let the federal government correct them and then see that they are enforced." Make no mistake about it; the public are not going to be hoodwinked much longer with this kind of thing. Employer and employee are insisting that it stop at once.
As I say, I am trying to express myself without prejudice. My sympathies are with the employers as well as with the employees. They all have their problems. They are being made to suffer because of a lack of cooperation between the controlling bodies. Nothing will be gained by setting up industrial relations committees unless all the conflicting interests are prepared to sit down and inject into their discussions a little bit of the milk of human kindness. I have simply tried to show by giving one example, and I could give many-I could recite some of my own personal experiences-how this thing works out.
I hear someone say, "Oh, you will not get anywhere with that sob stuff, with that sympathetic strain; it is a fight to the finish." That is what many are saying. That fight to the finish will ruin our very economy, and that is what I am alarmed about. I have talked with many union men and with many employers, especially during the last weeks when the committee was sitting, and I know that they are alarmed. With the consent of the house I should like to give a short summary.

Industrial Relations

I should like to recite a personal experience that occurred last Sunday morning which I think indicates what is in the hearts and minds of the people. A mother of four children ranging from six to fifteen years of age came to me last Sunday morning. She told me that she was desperate because her husband had become a different man during the last few months. She said, "I do not know whether this is the result of the war or not. He was always a faithful husband and took care of his family. We had our home nearly paid for from his earnings in one of the industries, and we weie very happy and proud over what we had accomplished." She said, "He seems to have been influenced in some way, something that I cannot lay my finger on. He does not seem to care whether his wife and family are provided for. He has said to me, 'I am not going to work any more than forty hours from now on, and I am going to have certain wages. If I don't get a certain amount of wages I am not going to work.' " This woman said to me, "I don't know what's come over this husband of mine, Mr. Lockhart. We are heading for disaster in my family. I understand there is a committee at Ottawa dealing with this question, and I am just giving you my personal experience. This husband of mine and his employer years ago used to work and live harmoniously together, and in those days he spoke highly of his employer. But someone has changed, Mr. Lockhart, and I am inclined to think that it is my husband who has changed at heart." That is just a humble woman's presentation of what is in the hearts and minds of people as a result of this sinister agitation that is going on all across this country.
The industrial relations committee have made a good report. They have done all they could. They carried on rational discussions under able guidance, and they have brought in their recommendations. If the government will only act upon them, those recommendations can form the basis of something valuable that can be done to improve labour relations. They represent the consensus of thirty-five men who worked conscientiously on that committee studying the situation, and if the government will live up to their responsibility, they will read, mark and inwardly digest the committee's report. I certainly will approve that report. I plead with all the factions who are involved in this terrific struggle for supremacy and who are putting forward formulas, be
they ten cents an hour increase or the forty-hour week-I plead with them: Stop, please, in the interests of the great public, in the interests of that poor mother with four children who is worrying her life out over her social insecurity. I say:	Stop flying at one
another's throats like pet bulldogs. Let us sit down and see if we cannot work out something to preserve our way of life, which at the present moment we are fighting to maintain.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to follow the argument of the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lockhart) but I hope he will not therefote assume that I agree with what he says. I most heartilj'' disagree with his point of view, but since it is only fractional in relation to the main issue I shall not spend time in replying to his argument now.
The question before this house is concurrence in the report of the industrial relations committee, which was appointed to investigate one of the major problems of modern civilization. There is no greater problem confronting Canada to-day or confronting any other capitalist nation on earth than this question of industrial strife, practically open warfare between the employers and the employees. It is not a new occurrence; it is not born of the war. It has been growing constantly for over two centuries, and as the problem develops and becomes more and more acute, strikes are more frequent and more violent, and so the problem grows.
I am sorry that I cannot support the report of the committee. While the committee may have done some fairly good work, I think on the whole it was a complete failure. It spent most of its time, and properly so, in investigating the steel strike. But it has shown fear or a lack of interest in bringing forward any solution or any suggestion of a solution for the steel strike or any other strike.
Several hon. members have said that the committee's chief value has been in the education which has been imparted to the public on industrial relations. I would just like to know, sir, what education that was. It imparted none to me, and I fail to see what it could have imparted to anyone else.
The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) gave I think the most lucid and comprehensive review of the entire proceedings of that committee. I was amused by his definition of industrial relations. I think there must have been some confusion in his mind between that natural impulse of human nature to improve the conditions of life and the means by which life is made possible,
Industrial Relations

and the real industrial warfare of modern civilization. At any rate his concept of industrial relations and of industrial unrest was put forward by analogy when he told us that when you saw a savage of the rough stone age fashioning a tool out of rock, that was industrial unrest; and when you saw some who had made a superior mousetrap, that also was industrial unrest. Well, we can stand a good deal of that kind of industrial unrest, I may tell my hon, friend. But the kind of industrial unrest which this committee was to deal with was a very different kind of unrest from the making of stone tools or the making of a mousetrap or anything else that may be implied in that analogy. The problem has been greatly accelerated by the very principle to which the hon. gentleman referred, namely, that every discovery and every new invention in our technological advance has but increased industrial unrest and made it more difficult for a large section of the public to live, whereas it should have made it much easier for them to live, and to live on a very much higher standard.
The hon. member for Calgary West quoted Mr. Conroy to the effect that all the world is going socialist or communist, and the hon. member for Calgary West agreed with that view. It seems that he thought the situation which threatened to terminate in socialism or communism so desperate that the Conservatives called a caucus, and the result of that Conservative caucus was the proposal of the hon. member for Calgary West which resulted in the committee's taking over this inquiry into industrial unrest. The hon. member proceeded to review the evidence; and without following him step by step in that review I immediately rushed to his conclusion, which was that nothing was proven: that was his conclusion. After all the investigation it has resulted in nothing. He said that he was not convinced that a case had been made out by Mr. Donald Gordon for a ten cent maximum increase in wages, but while he was not convinced that a case had been made out, he was so desperately afraid there might be something in it that he was utterly paralyzed and took no action in the committee on the matter. Apparently a majority of the committee did likewise. He was equally convinced that labour had failed to make out a case, and so "not proven" was the verdict of the hon. member for Calgary West in his summing up of the evidence before this committee.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to ask, was it not possible to prove, could not the committee have got the evidence to prove, that $33.60 a week, the amount asked by labour now on

strike, was the minimum required for the preservation of health and self-respect? Was it not possible to provide the evidence which would prove whether that amount was too great, or too little, or sufficient? Again: was it not possible to prove that the industry could or could not pay the amount of increase asked by the striking steel workers? I suggest to you, sir, that that is a matter for public hearing. That public hearing should be demanded by the house from now on in the case of every company which comes asking for an increase in prices.

Industrial Relations

As I said a few moments ago, industrial strife, which is now politely called "unrest," is of long standing, and it is growing progressively worse, because a strike anywhere affects people everywhere. We are so completely tied together in a network of industrial relations that when a strike takes place in one part of the country it affects practically all other parts of the economy. Also strikes are brought about more rapidly in these days because the effect of invention and technological progress is to speed up the cycle of production, and without a corresponding speeding up of the cycle of consumption there must be industrial chaos.
Of course the public interest cannot be ignored. A strike in a basic industry such as steel if it continues for any length of time, will most assuredly cause a shut-down in other industries. In addition, the public is interested because it wants goods, it wants to be served, and it does not want to see anything stop that service. But let me say, sir, that as well as having an interest in them the public must, accept some responsibility for these things. It is all very well for us to say that in the interests of the public, industry must go on no matter what happens. I would say that the public has a responsibility to see that industries go on, but it also has a responsibility to see that industries must not be allowed to continue to go on at the expense of the sweat and blood of the working people in it.
In reviewing the proceedings of the committee's study of the strike I cannot find that any attempt was made to deal with the causes of strikes generally, other than to say that apparently they are something which comes out of the head of a communist, that there are no real economic causes. Any committee which is going to find a formula for a situation of this kind surely must go a little deeper in its studies than this committee went. If strikes and industrial unrest are to be brought to an end, surely the causes of these things must be determined by any committee which inquiries into them.
I suppose it would not be well received by the house if at this time I were to give my views as to these causes. I shall refrain from doing so at this time in the hope that on some future occasion I shall have a better opportunity; but I cannot refrain from a criticism of the committee for failing to search for and find that cause, since the matter was referred to it. The economic causes of all strikes of the past and all that will happen in the future were not touched at all; therefMr. Irvine.]
fore we can hardly expect any formula of real value until these causes have been brought to the surface and removed.
I think I may conclude by saying that the large corporations in question in this strike have a very great influence on government.
I do not mean only on this government as a Liberal government; I mean on any government. Their economic position in the country is so powerful that they would have a similar influence on any government as long as that power remained in their hands. To make clear what I mean, I would say I have been looking over the great network of leading industrial and financial institutions of whose board the directors of the Steel Company of Canada and the other steel companies are members. After looking over that network I would say that the government of Canada could not successfully float a major loan without its assistance. If the government should find it necessary very shortly to float a major loan to absorb the surplus money which there are no goods to offset, or if the government should find it necessary to launch into great public undertakings for the winning of the peace as we did for the winning of the war,
I say that without the assistance of these directors and the companies they direct, that loan could not be successful. Therefore I say that the directors of these companies are part of the invisible government of Canada, and the invisible government is more powerful , than the visible government.
Before I sit down, Mr. Speaker, I say this session should not close until this steel strike is settled. There is nothing to be gained by merely approving the report of this committee. That will settle nothing. It will not even touch the subject. The situation is serious and is very likely to become more serious. Other great strikes are looming up. The industry of Canada is threatened with paralysis. This house represents the public of Canada, the common people of Canada. This parliament and this government have responsibilities which they must discharge. I say it would be criminal folly to pass this by lightly or to close this hQuse before this matter has been settled, whether that is done by sending the committee back to work or bv the government accepting a new policy and announcing it in this house, and going forth to put it into operation. That is largely for the government to decide, but that it should be decided one way or the other, and that this house should remain in session until this matter has been settled, I have not the slightest doubt in the world.

Mr. Speaker, I am going to emulate the hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Lennard), by being brief. There are only one or two points I wish to bring up, inasmuch as I sat through the sittings of the committee.
When the committee was appointed a crisis existed in the economy of the country. It dealt first with the steel strike in Hamilton. All other negotiations in connection with wages ceased in the major strikes across the
(Mr. Nicholson.]
countiy. In other words it was generally recognized that if this committee came out with a recommendation, it would apply all across the board. But during the meetings of the committee, any time we ever got near to coming out with a formula for settlement, it was brought to our attention in a very forceful manner that the committee had not been set up to settle anything. In other words, when negotiations had ceased all across the board, pending the adoption of some formula by that committee, all the committee did in the last five weeks in the light of present-day events was to dangle a carrot in front of the workers' noses. Now they have not even the carrot to sniff.
So far as I am concerned, if at any future time I have anything to do with such a committee I will first go out and tell the workers of this country, "Beware of it; pay no more attention to parliamentary committees". If in a crisis such as this a parliamentary committee representing parliament itself has no power whatsoever when all other machinery has broken down, then I say this country is getting into a pitiful state.
Throughout the meetings of the committee the point which was brought to my attention most forcibly was that labour was dealt with as though it were a cost factor in production- nothing more and nothing less; that the question was considered from the point of view that the laws of this country must be applied when private interests are in danger. It was not a case of the law coming down and dealing equally with one person as against another. The law comes down to protect the formula that labour is a cost factor in production.
Time and again the question w'as asked, "If markets fall and if profits go down, will you accept a lower wage, in view of the fact that at the present time in the face of rising costs you are demanding a rising wage? In other words when production becomes too great will you accept a smaller wage?" Well, if that line of argument continues under our present basis, the powers that be are going to find, to their sorrow, that labour is not just a cost factor m production, but that it is a social force. After we had sat for five or six weeks in the committee, trying to solve present problems, a minister of the crown says in the house that strikes have got to the point where they will solve themselves. In other words, what you are doing is allowing natural forces in society to drift; nothing "is", it is always "becoming".
When you say that strikes are getting to the point where they will solve themselves, and when a Minister of Labour says that we do not need the type of legislation we are

Industrial Relations
asking for and that we should have the same relationship as they have in Great Britain, where employees and employers recognize each other-if you admit that, you will also have to admit that we shall have to go through the history of British labour-capital relations. For all we know, we may be at that point in Canada which Great Britain had reached in 1926-and you will have a general strike on your hands.
Labour at the present time recognizes that the key point is Steleo. If the boss wins there, it means that they have the entering wedge to wreck the whole labour movement in this dominion. And labour, recognizing that, will be forced to use its economic strength; because labour is better educated in this country than it ever was before. They recognize it, from coast to coast, and they will pull thp pin on all industry. And remember this, that when a general strike breaks out it is not only an economic strike; it is a political force. Immediately it transforms itself into that, whether there be agitators then or not. Labour is forced to recognize that it is up against a state force-a state force that is saying, "You are a cost factor in production, and nothing more." When that comes out, what happens is that labour becomes politicized; it becomes a political force. Who gains control of that political force, we do not know. One thing we do know is that they will act in their own best interests, either slowly or with a great deal of speed as the case may be. That is the position labour is facing to-day. If a general strike is to come through the development of an unconscious drift in these affairs, I as a trade unionist and a member of the House of Commons will have to support it, inasmuch as it has been caused by the stupidity of government.

Mr. Speaker, the attention of the house should be called once again to some simple and straightforward truths about the matter we are now discussing. The industrial relations committee was asked by this house to deal with the present industrial unrest in Canada. While the terms of reference of the committee did not refer specifically to steel, it was clearly understood that therein was the most critical issue facing the country, and accordingly the committee devoted practically the whole of its time to the dispute with the steel companies. Surely it was the job of the committe to come to grips with that issue and make a report that would somehow settle the matter, but the simple fact is that the committee did not achieve a settlement of that dispute, nor has it made in its report to the house any recommendation that deals with the
basic issue. The report contains in a platitudinous way some recommendations that are all to the good, but those recommendations are offset, at least in the view of some of us, by the recommendation in clause 6 which organized labour regards as a retrograde step.
I listened a moment ago to the hon. member to my right, with whose general position I do not agree, and I heard him speak most strongly in support of labour unions being permitted to run their own affairs without outside interference. I for one am not satisfied that the wording of clause 6 of the report will not violate that very principle. The recommendations of the report are either platitudinous or questionable. Further, the report has the outstanding liability that it does not deal with the basic issue in the steel dispute, the question of wages, whether the ten cent straitjacket is to be applied or whether higher levels are to be agreed to.
For this house merely to indulge in the oratory we have had for the last two or three days and to concur in this report would in my view be a failure on its part to do its duty. If we go home without making some definite decision, then the members of this house will be partly responsible for the situation which now obtains.
There are two things which this House of Commons should do. First, it should register a protest over the failure of the committee to do its job. I listened to the glowing accounts of harmony in the committee, the praise of the chairman and all that, but the simple fact is that there is before us no recommendation from the committee with reference to the matter at issue, namely wage rates in steel. As I say, one of the things that we in this House of Commons must do is to protest in the most effective way we can against the failure of the committee to do its job.
The other thing which I feel this House of Commons should do at this time is to place the responsibility clearly where it lies, namely, on the shoulders of the government. If we merely concur in this report and go home, we shall have provided an out for the whole situation, and it can then go on from bad to worse. It is my intention before resuming my seat to move an amendment to the motion before the house, designed to give this house an opportunity to do two things; to register its protest against the failure of the committe to do its job. and to call upon the government to accept its responsibility and measure up thereto.
When I speak of government responsibility it is pertinent to ask in what way that responsibility lies. As has teen pointed out by the leader of this group and by others who

He asked the minister whether or not he was behind the action of the management of the steel company in driving trucks in and out of the plant despite potential injury to life and limb. The minister's reply was to the effect that every man's home was his castle and that he'regarded the right to go in and come out of a place of work in the same light. I do not take issue with that general statement, but the fact is that th'e kind of statements the minister has been making have had the effect of encouraging strike-breaking. Furthermore, they have had the effect of discolouring the situation as it exists at Hamilton. I was on the long-distance telephone to Hamilton myself about a quarter of an hour before the house met this morning. We have had telegrams continually and have kept in as close communication as we possibly could with Hamilton, and the information that is given to us is that at no time have the picket lines around that plant prevented ingress or egress of individuals in a normal orderly way. The trouble arises when large groups are moved in or out in a provocative manner, and I cannot help but notice the strange coincidence of these incidents taking place just now when this matter is being debated in the House of Commons. Many an individual I am told has gone in or out of the plant, and if individuals were to go in and out in an orderly way the workers who are inside the plant could come and go as much as they wish. The minister and the government generally by their attitude are helping to create the impression, and the press is responsible for it as well, that there is a group of lawless people among the strikers at Hamilton who are acting in such a way as to prevent the movement of people in and out of the plant without danger of bodily harm.
There are two reasons why the workers who are inside the plant at Hamilton do not want to come out. One is, of course, that they would not like their faces to be seen by their fellow workers. Any worker or trade unionist will know what I mean by that. The other reason that keeps these workers inside the plant is the triple pay they are receiving. When questions are asked about that, the minister's reply every time is to the effect that these people cannot get out, that they are kept in the plant by lawless strikers so-called, and that, I take it, is the reason why the government winks at this triple pay because it is thought that these men are com-

Industrial Relations
pelled to stay inside the plant. If the minister would be what he sometimes says he is, impartial; if he would not forever colour thing's against the workers, but give an honest statement of the situation as it stands, you would not have the kind of trouble that is there now. I suggest that the government's unwillingness to do anything about this triple pay underlines its responsibility for the present situation. The plant is now under government control. This means that the government, which has its wage ceiling policy, is a party to these greatly enhanced wage rates which the men inside are receiving. If that triple pay were stopped and it were generally known that the picket lines consist of individual persons between whom people can pass in and out, you would have the men coming out of that plant and going home in a normal way. Once they no longer were receiving triple pay, and once they had passed by the gaze of their fellow workers who are out on strike, some of them would not go back. That would make the situation a little more difficult for the company, but at least it would keep the law.
The situation is tense, but the kind of provocation that is going on at the present time involves the government in a responsibility on two counts. One is the general statement of government policy-the ten-cent limit-and the other is that the plant is now under government control, through a controller whose policies are provocative. When this situation obtains one cannot be surprised at questions, inflammatory questions if you wish so to describe them, being raised in the minds of labour. It is said that the purpose of the government is to uphold the price ceiling, but it is awfully hard to convince labour that that is the purpose of the government when in the steel industry itself a price increase of So a ton was granted. It is said that the thing the government fears most is inflation, and the Minister of Labour himself is most vigorous in his statements about the fear of inflation. Yet the situation as it is being allowed to develop is a much greater threat of inflation than a wage increase would be, even a greater increase than the steelworkers are asking. These professed motives seem so hollow to the workers, for the reasons I have indicated, that they get the notion . that there must be some other purpose-that either the government is deliberately out to weaken the position of the organized workers, or that it is being used by those who have such ideas. When a motion is made for concurrence in a report from a select committee, it is competent for the house to adopt it, reject it, refer it back to the committee with or without instructions, or decide that consideration of the report will take place "this day six months," as the hon. member can see by referring to Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms,. third edition, which cites a decision given by Mr. Speaker Rhodes on May 22. 1919, and reported at page 689, and at page 203. Mr. Speaker, I was not a member of this committee, but I should like to make a few general remarks on the subject of industrial relations and unrest. First of all, I should like to say that I have no intention of trying to embarrass the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). Whether or not we agree with him, I think we all feel, or at least we should feel
that he has a most responsible position and is carrying out a very thankless task. I do not profess to be a labour expert, so my remarks are going to be quite general in character. I have always felt that the Minister of Labour has the most difficult job in the government, and I think he comes in for more criticism than almost any other minister. This criticism is mainly by those who not only do not occupy positions of responsibility but have never occupied responsible positions. As I say, whether or not we agree with him he is entitled at this time to the sympathy of the house and the country at large.
It was the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) who opened the debate, and I have heard most of the speakers who followed him. My object in rising now is to speak on behalf of that section of labour which is more or less silent.
I gathered from remarks of previous speakers that labour is socialist or at least in favour of socialism. The C.C.F. group certainly assume that, but I have no real means of finding that out for myself, except that a year ago at the general election, if I remember aright-and correct me if I am wrong-the socialist candidates lost every deposit east of Winnipeg but one. That is to say, industrial Canada, the Canadian workers, when they had an opportunity to vote secretly, registered in no uncertain way the fact that they do not want to be under a socialist economy in Canada.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: You would not like to bet that that will last, would you?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
At the present time I am not making any comments on that. I merely state it as a fact. The reason I think that the Canadian workers have not yet fallen for socialism is that they value their individual freedom too much. I would like to make it perfectly clear that I am just as much a friend of labour as anyone in this house, and I certainly would fight for the right of the workers to strike. But it seems to me that if things continue as they are going to-day it is only a question of time when immediately there is a strike the government will be asked or told or commanded to step in and settle the strike. That is not my idea of freedom. Surely if it is the workers' right to strike, it is the workers' right to settle a strike, unless it happens to be that if the strike continued there would be a national emergency such as was created this summer when the railway men in the United States struck. But generally speaking I respect the workers' right to strike as their most valuable freedom. Once they lose that, it seems that their freedom is gone.
The end of socialism is, of course, complete government ownership and government con-
Industrial Relations

trol, and wherever you have that, there can be no strikes and there can be no unions in the sense that we know them. Therefore I defend the right of the workers to contract out. I defend the right of everybody to contract out. If they do not like a job or a situation it is their privilege and their right to contract out of it and not to be compelled to accept conditions which they do not care to accept.
There is no doubt that there is and has been in the Liberal party and in the Conservative party a trend towards socialism. So far as the Liberal party is concerned I put it down to the fact that the economic advisers of the Liberal party are and have been for a considerable time recruited from the-London school of economics, which is purely a socialist training school. It was founded by Fabian socialists and it was financed by German international finance. That London school of economics has supplied the economic advisers at the present time and for some time past for the Liberal party. I read an editorial on a speech made by the Hon. Mr. Crerar the other day in the senate. He seemed to regret the passing of the old-time Liberalism. Well, where you have Liberal policies founded on the ideas of such men as Harold Laski, Mr. Rasminsky, Doctor Marsh and the rest of the London school of economics, you certainly do have a departure from the old Liberal school.
I should like to make a few remarks on a free economy. These ideas are not new, but they are worth repeating, and they are certainly pertinent to the subject under discussion.
If free to do so producers always try to sell dear and consumers always try to buy cheap. These instincts are as old as the human race and I suppose they will continue to the end of the chapter. For example, every workingman, who is a producer in the sense that he sells his labour, naturally sells his labour for as much as he can get for it. The wife of every workingman is a consumer and if she is a good housewife she tries to buy as cheaply as possible, or at least she sees to it that she gets either the most or the best for her money. When prices fall, consumption is stimulated but production is discouraged. At what level will most goods be produced and consumed? When you have a rise in prices, production is stimulated but consumption is discouraged. But for every commodity every day of the year there is a point where production and consumption meet one another on an- equal basis. That point can only be determined as a result of the day to day transactions of millions of buyers and sellers meeting and doing business freely with one
[Mr. Jaquea.l
another. This is the point of greatest production and greatest consumption, and this is economic democracy. Whenever governments or monopolies of producers or of labour fix prices, rents, dividends or wages above or below' that free meeting point, production and consumption get out of balance and we get what we have to-day, a general economic paralysis. It stands to reason that the millions of individuals who comprise the nation can judge for themselves what prices they will pay for how many and what kind of goods they want, and consequently how many goods should be produced. Everybody knows that, and each individual is the. only person who can know it. Every individual knows what he wants, and every individual knows what he wants to pay, and the individual is the only person who can know that; everybody else can only guess. That is the free market; and whenever governments interfere to control a free market, whether it be in the field of production, consumption or labour, the result is always the same, a loss of human liberty and human happiness and satisfaction. The only alternative to the free market is an iron control over every phase of the nation's life by the gestapo and the concentration camp, and that is the history of socialism, applied socialism as it has worked out in Europe, the only place in w'hich it has been worked out. In a free market, if one charges too much and buying falls off, competitors will charge less or offer a better product and so take the market away from him. A free market is a democratic market; it is a continuous meeting where every citizen every day votes with his or her dollars what he wants and what he wants produced. His dollars are always looking .for the best bargain, that is the best and the most for the least expense. This forces the producers to offer the best or the most for the money, or go out of business to make room for those who do. The result is an ever-rising scale of living, and that is why the freer the country the higher its standard of living, and that is why the living standards are low in dictator countries; that is the reason to-day for the tie-ups in such industries as building. All the way down the line, industry is held up because producer and consumer cannot meet in mutual agreement as buyer and seller but must wait on the dictates of some bureaucrat who has no real or personal interest in the matter.
So much for a free economy. I believe the sooner we get back to a free economy the sooner we shall bring real prosperity and happiness to the people of Canada.

Industrial Relations
A few words about the communist influence in industrial unrest. As I say, I was not a member of this committee, so my remarks do not apply specifically to this committee. I am making general remarks which I can back up with statements by people in authority. I should say, of course, that labour is very largely international to-day, and certainly most of the Canadian labour unions are either controlled by or affiliated with the labour unions of the United States. If that is incorrect perhaps the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) will correct me.
Let me quote the Attorney General of the United States, speaking this summer to the Canadian Bar Association:
No one but a crackpot can be deluded by what we see going on to-day. One of the greatest dangers in my opinion to the civil liberties of our fellow citizens, and one which should be taken literally by all the members of our profession, is the method of communism and fascism to shackle democracy by indirection. We know there is a national and international conspiracy to divide our people, to discredit our institutions, and to bring about disrespect of our government. We know full well what communism and fascism practise,-sometimes one taking the cloak from the other. We know that in the black bible of their faith they seek to capture the important offices in the labour unions, to create strikes and dissensions, and to raise barriers to the efforts of lawful authorities to maintain civil peace. I am told that in the councils of many labour unions, wherein deliberations are screened from the public, identical tactics, staged with acute skill, are used to disrupt, disconcert proceedings in the hope that the communists or fascists-for I see no difference in them-may achieve final power. Small groups of radicals, well coached in a prearranged plan, are using party line methods in identical activity so that they can speak to the people as a whole, not in open avowal of their aims, but with the voice of the honest working man. No country on earth and no government can long endure this vicious attack. I say to you that they are driving law enforcement in this country to the end of its patience. They are driving good Americans to the end of their patience.
That was the statement of Attorney General Thomas Clark, of the United States of America. Then there is a statement I should like to read which I take from the committee of un-American activities of the Congress of the United States, printed in Washington, 1946, page 48:
A majority of ill-informed members of industry, finance, education and religious institutions sneer at the power and progress of the communist party in the United States. These same individuals often point out that the communist party is a legal party and not a member of a subversive movement and is merely the expression of a small alien minority. To indicate the extent to which these persons have been misled by the propaganda agencies operating under the guidance of communists and fellow travellers in America, we present the statement made by Joseph Stalin, nominal head of
the communist party in Russia and the dominant figure of the movement throughout the world.
This is Premier Stalin's statement:
"I consider that the communist party in the United States of America is one of the few communist parties to which history has given decisive tasks from the point of view of the world revolutionary movement. The revolutionary crisis has not yet reached the United States, but we already have knowledge of numerous facts which suggest that it is aproaching. It is necessary that the communist party should be capable of meeting the moment of crisis fully equipped to take the direction of future class wars in the United States of America. You must prepare for that, comrades, with all your strength and by every means you must constantly improve and bolshevize the American communist party. You must forge real revolutionary leaders of the proletariat who will be capable of leading the millions of American workers towards the revolutionary class wars."
This statement has never been repudiated and is officially recorded on page 17 of house report No. 2 of the 76th Congress.
The real communist threat is not from the few members of the communist party who are honest enough to declare their true colours, but from the innumerable what I call "fellow-travellers". They remind me of the unfortunate people who carry typhoid. They do not have the disease themselves, but they spread it. There are a lot of people who may not be communists in the full sense of the word, but they spread a lot of communism.
The hon. member for Calgary West said something about the spread of socialism and communism, but I did not hear him say anything about stopping the spread of it. He did complain of the newspapers. He said they were always ready to strangle the birth of a new idea. I have not heard any new ideas expressed in this debate. There is nothing new in socialism. It is as old as slavery. The hon. member for Calgary West comes from the province which did give birth to a new idea.

No, I am not selling it, but I shall open the eyes of the hon. member if he is not entirely blind. Here are some notes I took from this article:
Who is the real author of "Under Cover", the well-known smear book? On the cover of the book is the name-John Roy Carlson, but who is John Roy Carlson? Where did the smear bund dig him up? The author of "Under Cover" admits using Carlson as a pen name. But Carlson is only one of several pen names. His real name is Avedis Boghos Derounian, an Armenian immigrant. The name of the author of "Under Cover" is given as Derounian, alias Carlson, alias Paige, alias Decker, alias Pagnanelli, et cetera. But the real author is the communist smear bund. By means of Carlson and other hired hands, such as Walter Winchell and using "patriot" as an alias, the bund's purpose is to smear, as agents of Hitler, any native Americans of untarnished reputation, loyalty and eminence who actively oppose communism and internationalism. In 1935 Carlson edited a communist sheet mainly to extol the bolshevik conquest of his native Armenian home, smearing all who did not agree with his employers. In 1938 he was hired by the anti-defamation league and later by the "Friends of Democracy" as one of their numerous pimps. He went around people suspected of anti-semitism, encouraged them to make slurring remarks and then reported the remarks to his blackmailing employers as samples of anti-semitism. He issued an antisemitic sheet of his own containing the vilest attacks on the Jews in order to needle people to say anything he could report to the alien racketeers who paid him.
"Under Cover" pretends to expose a number of subversive groups in America, but it never once mentions the activities of such people as those exposed by our own Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The very purpose of the book is to keep communist spies and agents under cover. The methods are the usual smear employed by communists and fellow travellers, and by the anti-defamation league. The technique is that used by all blackmailers-to compromise decent honourable people by associating them with those guilty of the offence with which they intended to smear their victims. In "Under Cover" the victims were the opponents of internationalism, communism, and the opponents of certain new dealers.

Carlson was hired by the "Friends of Democracy", operated by Rex Stout, former editor of the New Masses and Leon Birkhead, both active communist workers.
So much for John Roy Carlson. Blackmailers are rightly detested as most odious and dangerous criminals. They are character assassins preying on the respectable, but vulnerable, members of society. Private citizens are protected against blackmail by most severe and drastic penalties. Men in public life enjoy no protection against such blackmailers as the Carlsons, Winchells, and their employers, the communists, the anti-defamation league, the political zionist leaders, all working to defeat the ends of justice, freedom and Christianity, silencing or disarming their opponents by smearing them with fascism and anti-semitism. Honest and sincere patriots must face these blackmailers or abandon their principles.
To give you some idea of the extent of the activities of these subversive agents, let me quote the words of the national director of the anti-defamation league, referred to by Mr. Flynn in the article in the Times-Herald:
The programme of education we have developed covers every media for improving the human mind.
Improving the human mind!
In several fields which have engaged the league's attention we have developed the outstanding agencies of America. We have the greatest speakers' bureau ever organized in this country. We have the outstanding radio programmes in all the history of American radio.
Such as Walter Winchell I suppose.

Including "Under Cover." Finally, they have succeeded in organizing to convert the world to internationalism and totalitarianism, according to the doctrines of Karl Marx, the psychoanalysts and the political Zionists.

I thought I had made the point that a great deal-I would not like to say how much-of the industrial unrest in North America, which would include Canada, is due directly to the propaganda and active work of communists. They work under cover, and I was trying to take off the cover in order to expose this thing for what it is. That was my only purpose, but now I am through with the communists.
Before I sit down I should like to be a little constructive. Having been a little critical so far I should like to close my remarks in a constructive way. I should like to reiterate something I said in an address not long ago, dealing with the solution of these problems of industrial unrest. I speak in the most general way, because I am not referring to any particular strike, such as the steel strike, or even to Canada alone. I am speaking of industrial unrest all over the North American continent or, if you like, all over the world. It is not a question of capitalism or socialism; of "cartelism" or communism. Capitalism of itself, is no cure for socialism, any more than socialism is the cure for capitalism; the blind cannot lead the blind. The truth lies between the extremes of right and left. It is not a question of peace based on full employment. We face a new age; not merely a machine age, but a power-machine age. That means an age of increasing leisure, not of increasing employment. We cannot reverse our program; we must not confuse means with ends. The real purpose of industry is to create goods and service, not jobs. As Ruskin said, "consumption is the crown of production."
We face an age of real plenty and, therefore, we cannot remain slaves of a money economy which was developed during the ages of real scarcity. We dare not prolong our orthodox, but obsolete, financial system of sound, scarce, money by creating artificial scarcities of goods. Our money must reflect facts, not fallacies. Dollars are economic ballots, and when we spend dollars we are voting for the reproduction of what we buy. In this way only can the people plan and obtain the goods and services they really want to 'have. But by their "planned economy' the socialists would dictate to the people what, when and
how much they should consume. Socialists condemn profit, but defend interest. The financiers and socialists-Shylock and Marx-[DOT] are monopolists; they plan to centralize the control of the production of money and of goods. If we are to have world peace, "foreign trade" must be regarded as trade, an exchange of what we cannot consume for what we cannot produce. Favourable trade balances are a fallacy, and the struggle to obtain them has been a main cause of wars in the past. If we are to be really free, all our citizens must be regarded as shareholders of the nation as a going concern and, as such, entitled to share in the national profits, distributed by means of national dividends. Taxation should not be imposed for revenue, but for the purpose of regulating the supply of money. Governments might lend but should never borrow. To say there is only so much money is equivalent to saying there are only so many tons, or miles. The poor are not poor because the rich are rich; that is another socialist fallacy. There is plenty for all. We have solved the problem of production, we must now solve the problem of distribution, or perish in the attempt. We cannot serve two masters; we cannot serve God and usury. If we value anything more than freedom we shall lose our freedom.
