Coming from the industrial district in Ontario where the trade union movement in Canada started, I wish to say a few words this afternoon in connection with these proposals. Some have complained that the day is being wasted. That is not so. Peace in industry is the greatest problem facing this parliament. That is what parliament was called together to consider last March. Some of those to my left, the C.C.F., have been pleading the case for the farmer and agriculture, and in some respects it may be fairly said they forgot all about the industrial workers of the cities and towns of this country, who are employed in these heavy industries which have done so much for this country. This committee was appointed to establish peace in industry. That was a large order, because after every great war we have had the same dislocation of labour and of trade and industry and commerce. I would not be altogether prepared to say it was the fault of the government. In fact it would be very unfair to say that, because the textbook writers after all great wars have agreed for the last hundred years that this may or may not be so.
Hon. members on this side of the house have always been a trade union party, so far as I have known them. We are the only real
Industrial Relations

protectionist party in the house-national protection for labour, protection for the farmers, protection for agriculture and for industry, protection for trade and commerce, for retail stores and for manufacturers of all kinds, and national production brought up to date to meet the spirit of the age and time. Our maxim has been: our own work for our own workmen; our own markets for our own products. Those are the two cardinal principles which have built up this country.
As an hon, member who entered this parliament several years ago, it is my belief that the committee deserves the thanks not only of the House of Commons but of the government of the country and of labour and industry for the work it did. I do not agree with everything contained in the report as far as it goes, because it is well known that after every great war there has been industrial unrest in Canada and the world over.
The committee was given power to call witnesses and to examine them on oath. The Addington administration in 1801 faced industrial strife and faced unrest. They faced it in the dark days of the industrial revolution in England. They faced it in that old town hall in Birmingham, which was somewhat destroyed a while ago, where John Bright and Joseph Chamberlain and all those great men and orators who had something to do with the redeeming the lot of the workers of that land, had their say. That was the condition at the time of Shaftesbury, in 1847in those days the intolerable conditions among the working classes after the industrial revolution in the thirties led to labour and social reforms all along the line. One has only to read Green's "History of England" to understand the terrible state of affairs in those days, a time when women, and children of only eight or nine years of age, were working down in the mines, taking out the coal, in a living tomb with disease rampant. Trades unionism was a blessing to the land.
The city of Toronto has been a pioneer in its relations with labour. We have a splendid body of manufacturers who developed the industrial side of the city, and who comprise some of our leading and most patriotic citizens. We have, on the whole, as heads of our labour movements sane and sensible labour men. I had to aid in settling about twenty or thirty strikes, large and small, following the last war and during it. I remember a strike of the old Toronto Street Railway, and during the strike I appealed to the greatest labour leader this continent ever produced, Mr. Samuel Gompers, who at that time was president of the American Federation of Labour. He came to our city and the strike was settled

in about half a day. He advocated that the strikers be law-abiding, that they carry out peaceful picketing, and carry out their other duties peacefully, in a lawful manner. He appealed to other classes in the community to use sanity, a spirit of good will and wisdom, not to make inflammatory speeches, not to attack industry, and not to attack the police force. He said that police officers were only doing their duty as they saw it in the various cities of our country.
I was police commissioner and chairman of the board for many years in Toronto, and I can say that we had very little of that kind of trouble. For many years in the house I have been advocating a national policy for labour in Canada and for peace in industry. The report of the committee deals with many important matters. Indeed I believe it is the most important labour document we have had since the days of'the Bennett administration. If there was one administration in this country which stood up for the industrial workers in the cities and towns of Canada and also for the white-collar workers; if there was one administration which was the pioneer of this type of document for the benefit of the working classes, it was the Bennett administration, which set up the committee on price spreads which investigated these matters and brought down an important report and led to splendid reforms to improve the lot of the toilers and of industry and private enterprise, the creator of employment.
We have had collective bargaining in Canada for some time; they had it in England after the last war and before it. I do not believe altogether in section 6. I appreciate fully what was said by my hon. friend and brother party member who has done so much of this work, the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith). I remember him when he was a student in our city, and I know he was interested in this problem even in those days. He is a most warm-hearted man, and one who takes part in many spheres of activity to aid the common man, for whom he has a profound sympathy. He is a man who deserves to be listened to, and one who has won the esteem not only of the people of western Canada but of people throughout the country. I agree with him when he claims "the right for every man to run his own life in his own way." That is what I have been contending for, and that is what the price spreads inquiry contended for. I would rather under section 6, see the chief electoral officer handle a vote in industry in this matter than the Minister of Labour who has had such a hard task after a gigantic war. We have a chief electoral

Industrial Relations
officer, and all of us have had something to do with him. I believe he should be placed in charge of the balloting in industry. No matter what his politics are, he has always given each of us a fair and decent show. I believe the chief electoral officer would avoid government interference and so aid the Minister of Labour.
As a friend of labour, in some respects I am sorry to see this recommendation in section 6, because to a great extent these industrial disputes are matters for the consideration of the government. I have had experience with many such disputes, probably as many as any other hon. member now in the house-but perhaps not as many as the Minister of Labour, with his vast labour experience, because he was in the labour movement for many years, in two cities-Hamilton, and where he is now. I have followed his career with interest.
I can. tell you this, that we shall never have peace in industry in this country until we have a national policy for labour and for industry. I have, since 1922 advocated such a national policy of protection to solve all our economic problems from the Yukon to the maritime provinces. I have recommended a national policy for labour, a national policy which should provide protection bonuses, subventions and subsidies on grain, coal, steel, iron and other important commodities. I was almost alone in my advocacy at that time. Only in this way can labour hope to get a proper share of the returns in our peace-time economy; only in this way can industry and private enterprise get their fair share of aid.
I have always listened with great respect to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) the leader of the C.C.F., who said that the ten-cent limit would place labour in a straitjacket. No hon. member, no decent citizen, wants to see any man who works for his living placed in a straitjacket. I have great respect for the hon. member, but I do not think he or any other hon. member wants to see either labour or private enterprise in a straitjacket.
Some of our friends want a complete system of nationalization, socialization and public ownership. That works all right in connection with light, heat and power, and with some forms of transportation, but when it is expanded it cannot be successful unless it operates as a monopoly. That is the only way that public ownership, both past and present, of which I have long been an advocate, has been successful.
There have been better working conditions since I first entered the city council in Toronto.
Our friends sitting to the left are trying to pacify Europe. The hon.. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) went over to Russia to try to pacify the Russians and Marshal Stalin-and here we are in the 106th day of the session, but the government cannot pacify a few workmen. That is how it is in. some of the industries in the country. The hon. member went over to preach the gospel to Stalin and company-limited and unlimited. No doubt while he was over there he learned some of the new modern tricks in the political trade-because there are always some tricks to learn in this trade used by politicians. We are all politicians; some of us saw the sun, and some did not. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is over there trying to pacify Europe. A whole carload of them has gone, including the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Claxton). He is in Paris, but he may show up in. Oslo or in almost any city of the seven seas. I think there is plenty of room for them, at home, to maintain peace in industry in this country, the most important problem before parliament.
A discussion of this matter is certainly not a waste of time, because these workers are people who pay taxes-taxes which are intolerable. I can tell you this, that I walked along streets in my constituency, and in the constituencies of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and other Toronto members the other night, and on those streets I saw members of the working classes shopping. It was raining pretty hard that night and the price ceiling had huge holes shot in it. Many of the people who came to this country only a few years ago are making fabulous sums out of the sale of vegetables and fruit, but the farmer is not getting it. The ceiling has been shot full of holes for the consumer, and prices are soaring on consumer goods of all kinds. It is well known that the price ceilings are connected economically with the wage ceilings, and that is one thing the committee had to consider in making its report. Where do we go from here after this report?
We are back to where we are kicking the football around again. We are in the football season now. The government kicked the football over to the committee on July 14 and we have now kicked it back. The onus of settling this strike is on the government as long as they are the government. I think the committee was very fair to the government because it was an exceedingly laborious task it had to do, it was a tiresome, wearisome and thankless task. I went into the committee two or three times and I saw it w'as a tiresome, wearisome and thankless job they were doing
Industrial Relations

in trying to help the government out of the trouble they were in. All governments have had to face this situation after every war.
Where do we go from here, with this committee report, uniting price ceilings and wage control? The onus is back on the government. We would be wise as the House of Commons to wind up our business by Saturday night and give the government a chance to deal with this problem and settle this strike. We are just wasting our time here, and the minister is not able to deal with this important matter. The onus is on the government, not on the exodus or only those who are travelling the seven seas, but those who are home, the home guard. The home guard is dwindling. Those who have been left at home have to face the toughest job which this government has had for a long time, to wind up this session and to formulate a labour code that will work after such a terrible war and bring about peace in industry.
The onus is on the government so far as it is the government of the day to solve this problem. This problem is not going to be solved by adopting brass-band methods of conducting a strike inquiry or by intimidation of the workers and private enterprise, or by calling in the police. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that trouble occurred in the city of Montreal a few years ago. The enforcement of federal laws should be placed in the hands of the Attorney General of Canada under section 91. It should not be necessary to tax real estate in order to provide a police force in Hamilton.
Another thing I cannot understand is that it was considered necessary by the steel industry and the labour union to treat this matter as a unit of industrial strife in the three plants. The conditions prevailing in Nova Scotia are different from those prevailing in Hamilton and Sault Ste. Marie. They are separate propositions all together. I think a great mistake was made in the unions handling it in this way. In Sault Ste. Marie and Hamilton they have cheap light, power and urban transportation and the cost of their carfares, water and civic services, and food is much less. In the maritimes they are faced with heavy freight charges, and then the system of taxation there is different. In Ontario there is cheap light and power available for almost every barn in the province, and we have cheap fares on our street cars. Domestic lighting is available for the home of the working man, and the cost of this service has been cut in three and four. For about 94 cents a unit a working man is able to light his house. Then they have extended the facilities for

cooking into the kitchens of the working classes of this province. In these disputes law and order should be maintained at any cost.
We had some trouble during the street railway strike and we had some trouble during the last war. But law and order must be maintained, as President Gompers said when we settled the street car strike. So far as this particular proposition goes, I sympathize with labour and I also sympathize with the employers as they are to-day. You must consider the cause and effect of these strikes. As I said before, business men are conscious of the heavy task that awaits them in reconversion so that Canada may recover quickly. Industry and labour in Canada have worked wonders in war, and can in peace also. Canada needs stability to speed the delivery of all classes of goods and meet market demands so as to aid peace-time economy in employment, supply civilian needs and restore as soon as possible living standards and defeat inflation and black markets. With the lessons industry learned in Canada in war, it should be much easier to work out reconversion. All irksome controls must go, and we must remove the shackles from industry, large and small. Business men must have complete freedom if they are to succeed under private enterprise. We should see an end to government controls and in that way give them more of a chance to provide full employment, and labour and capital a fairer share of our peace-time economy.
I am sorry to say that that has not happened, and one of the results is this strike. There is no doubt that the committee never should have summoned Donald Gordon or Mr. Brockington to handle matters such as this. I believe that the more the government kept away from it, the more chance there would be for the employers and employees to settle this question. On April 1, when I saw the unrest and that May day was coming, I asked this question:
What action has been taken by the government to set aside, by proclamation, some Sunday for a day of prayer for the promotion of peace in industry, in view of the need of reconversion in industry from war to peace economy.
The government replied that the suggestion was being noted, but that at present this did not appear to be a matter requiring action by the government. I notice they are adopting this programme in the mother country, and I am reminded of the town hall in Birmingham where John Bright and Joseph Chamberlain and others spoke shortly after the industrial revolution. I think this suggestion should be carried out on Labour day, a week from Sunday. The government should

Industrial Relations
consider setting aside, Sunday, September 1, as a day of national prayer for the promotion of peace and industry and to urge the necessity of such industrial peace to aid reconversion in industry from war to peacetime economy and aid the production of all kinds of consumer goods. I hope such a proclamation will be issued. When a well-known Canadian divine was referring to the town hall in Birmingham he mentioned that a celebrated labour leader had once said that he never entered an industrial conference without engaging in a season of prayer. God's spirit was always invoked in order that satisfactory results might be obtained. I think there is a lot in that, especially in times like these.
There are many important matters that need consideration by parliament. These strikes are caused largely by the working classes not being able to get into decent houses. That is the result of this silly rental control policy. We see letter after letter in the newspapers-there were three or four in the Toronto papers last night-complaining about the condition of those who buy and cannot get into what they buy. That is one of the causes of this strike. Then these working people are faced with high food prices. The danger of inflation at the moment is due to a shortage of supplies. That shortage has been largely brought about by the war. The government has, in my opinion, had a different policy in different provinces in regard to a price ceiling on wages. In British Columbia, in the dispute which Mr. Justice Sloan settled, an increase of fifteen cents was granted. That was in April or May. Now in August in Ontario an increase of ten cents is offered. Mistakes have been made, undoubtedly, but the government is not the only one to make mistakes. Mistakes are bound to be made after every war. The government's determination to hold price ceilings at all costs, when holes were shot in the ceilings has been responsible for strikes and the demand for higher wages. The line was held for a time, but it was only held in the days of stress and strain by granting the wartime cost of living bonus, subventions and subsidies, and other temporary benefits at great cost to the country and industry and the consumer.
We should enforce what labour laws we have, and if they are not right we should amend them to meet modern conditions. A few months ago the subsidy of two cents a quart was taken off milk, and the prices of the produce which the market gardeners bring
into the cities are going sky-high, without any price regulation at all. No wonder there is a demand for higher wages.
So far as the report of the committee is concerned there are four cardinal things the committee forgot to remember: Never legislate against human nature; trust the people and they will trust you; always tell the people the truth; do not be afraid to tell.the people you have made a mistake. The people do not expect their leaders to be infallible or to be gods and I am glad that my hon. friend the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) admitted the other night that he had had a change of mind. How can we develop the natural resources of this country when we have strikes continually occurring in basic industries like steel, coal, iron, base metals and everything else?
We have representatives over in Paris at the present time attending a conference about peace and disarmament. That is desirable, no doubt, but peace in industry at home is also sorely needed. After every war there is a lot of dislocation and all kinds of social problems to solve, which, if not solved properly, will cause strikes. Suspicion should be removed, suspicion not only abroad but also at home, because it tends to poison the thoughts in man. The removal of suspicion would aid industry and bring about stability, so that our people can go on confidently to better things. While not forgetting conferences abroad, let us have conferences at home for the very worthy object of peace in industry. Home should be the true place of peace and shelter from all injury, terror, want, doubt and unemployment. It is not home if it does not provide that.
Why should we reserve all our discussions on peace and security for Paris and the continent of Europe and forget about peace at home? Some of those who preached pacifism abroad failed to heed the cries for peace at home. Some of the best leaders of labour have uttered the same sentiments-not to forget peace at home-and I admire their courage, because these labour leaders are trying at the same time to carry out their duties to those they represent and that greater community their countiy.
I am urging all our citizens to plead for a truce in industrial strife. In the middle ages, when the whole of Europe was on fire, one part against another, men of good will strove in vain to get what the historians of the middle ages called a truce of God which would enable the people to settle their differences and live like brothers. I should like to see such a truce in this country to bring about peace in industry, so that we may remove all

Industrial Relations
differences and join in unison with all our strength to lead the people of this country to a happier and better collective security at home.
Governments sometimes can do little. These reforms must come from the people themselves and from free enterprise. Labour and private enterprise should take off their coats and work out a solution, of their troubles, because they can do it better than the state can, Let them put the state out of their minds and get down to it to-day, so that we may have peace in industry in every corner of this country. A breach of peace in industry means suffering from employment. All that could be avoided if capital and labour tried to understand each other.
I have felt that it would be a real'help to employers and employees to have a neutral person preside at industrial conferences, some man well qualified by character and ability and with an independent outlook who would inspire confidence. A person of such standing I have found in practice has always enabled the two parties to get together with ease and freedom and with a hope of ultimate success. Not only have wages to be studied, but the relationship between price ceilings and wage controls must not be lost sight of. Industrial disputes should be the concern of statesmen, because such disputes follow after every great war. Trade in our country has always depended on initiative and free enterprise and the willingness of our people, men and women, to embark their savings in industry. The element of uncertainty after every great war in industry is a great problem.
I do not believe there is any royal road to the solution of industrial strife any more than there is any royal road to learning. The government have no doubt made mistakes, and thejr have come in for some criticism. So has the opposition, the C.C.F. and all other parties. This steel strike is already having a serious effect upon business, and I hope that we shall conclude our business here very rapidly so as to give the government a chance to bring this strike to an end as soon as possible.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened attentively to the numerous speeches made on this subject, and I wish to offer my own views. They are, I must admit, far from being those of an expert in the matter.
In this debate so far, various opinions or suggestions have been made, some very constructive, others less so, but I do not think this problem can be solved by making speeches. What is needed is action without further delay.

The committee on industrial relations has made recommendations to this house, and in my opinion the most important of these recommendations is the one relating to a labour code. In this connection opinions seemed unanimous, and I hope that hon. members have given careful consideration to these suggestions. However, we must not forget the numerous angles of this problem.
The main obstacle to having a labour code is the result of our own constitution and is the conflict of jurisdiction between the various provinces and the Canadian parliament. The committee recommends that a dominion-provincial conference be called in order to draft legislation in this respect. I agree with this recommendation, provided that the provinces come here with a real desire for understanding, and I say this because our previous dominion-provincial conferences did not meet with great success.
The labour problem of this country is a national problem and, therefore, concerns as much the provincial legislatures of each province as it concerns the federal parliament. Each premier of each province should be ready to shoulder his responsibility in this respect. The strikes which affect our national economy to-day affect also all the provinces from British Columbia to the maritime provinces. I think, Mr. Speaker, that in the past there has been too much politics brought into the settlement of our national problems and in the discussions of our dominion-provincial relations. When the federal government wanted to make suggestions for the settlement of these problems, the provinces accused the federal government of attacking provincial autonomy.
A few days ago, the premier of Ontario, the Hon. George Drew, said in a public address that his government was seeking to have the federal government hold another dominion-provincial conference and he-Mr. Drew-was suggesting that this conference should deal also with our labour problems. The same suggestion has been made in the newspapers and by public men of this country, but I suggest that if the provinces want so much understanding between the federal government and the provincial governments they should, for once, themselves take the initiative. It is all very nice and good to say that it is up to the federal government to assemble the provincial ministers in a conference, but I do not think this initiative should come only and solely from this government. Why do the provincial ministers not get together on their own initiative and first agree among themselves before coming to Ottawa? Then, if the dominion-provincial

Industrial Relations
conference later fails, this failure would not rest with the central government only, since the provinces, would have taken their share of responsibilities in calling the meeting.
I am sure that, if the provinces come here after having discussed matters among themselves, an understanding with the federal government will be much easier to reach, since the provinces will be unanimous and will have reached an agreement among themselves before conferring with the central authorities. Then politicians will not be able to go around and say that Mr. King's conference has failed, if a failure should occur; but the people of Canada will know that, if agreement is not reached, the fault rests with no particular political party or no particular government, unless one of these governments fails to envisage the problem in the light of the national interest. Up to now it seems to me that the provinces have prevented the central government from taking action to solve our national problems, on the grounds of provincial autonomy; but when the consequences of these unsolved problems appear they throw it into the lap of the federal government as they are doing to-day, and say, "settle them." I do not think this is the way to arrive at the solution of our "national problems. Let the provinces take the initiative now and see if they can do better than the federal government has done up to now.
If I may offer suggestions regarding this labour code, I would suggest that uniform legislation be drafted by the provinces according to their own views and ambitions first and submitted afterwards for discussion in a dominion-provincial conference and that, after an agreement is reached on the proposed legislation, various provincial governments make it law in their respective province. This will be one way to eliminate the conflict of jurisdiction, since this national labour code would be enacted by the various legislatures independently. We federal members were told during the debate on redistribution that we did not represent our respective provinces. We should, therefore, to-day leave the floor to our provincial representatives in this respect.
There has been much talk recently about the danger of spreading communism in this country, and it has been asserted that communistic activities are taking place in our labour unions. I think this assertion is true, and I would suggest that, in order to curb these activities, which, to my mind are most detrimental to Canada, labour unions of this country should be exclusively Canadian in character. In order to achieve this end, I respectfully submit that our proposed labour
code should recognize only exclusively Canadian unions and make it compulsory for any labour union to incorporate itself under our laws with definite powers and definite obligations also. I know that many are opposed to the incorporation of labour unions, but I think we should have had it a long time ago. We are criticizing the government for delegating its powers to boards or commissions, but we do not seem to realize that labour unions to-day have more authority in the labour field than the government ever had. We have recently seen examples of labour unions who defied the government, took the law into their own hands and dictated their wishes to the whole of the country. These same unions have no responsibility whatsoever, having no legal existence. I believe that bodies which control most of our national economy should be responsible bodies and should come within the provisions of our laws. If ever a delegation of powers was made it was when we permitted such unions to act in this country. Public bodies like individuals should abide by the laws of the country according to the great principle of our democratic world that everybody is equal before the law. Why make an exception in the case of labour unions?
I know some hon. gentlemen will object by saying that this will prevent our local organization from taking part in the international organization, for the welfare of workers all over the world. I do not think this will be the case, since our national unions or local unions could do just as they did before and contribute to the international labour organization, and I see no objection there.
Before closing these few remarks, I wish again to emphasize the importance of the national character of this problem and of the necessity for immediate action. Strikes are to-day paralyzing the whole economy of this country. It is not only one class of our society that is affected, but the whole of our national economy and the whole of our Canadian society. Let us, therefore, put aside, for the sake of our country, our individual views and opinions, and let us look at. the problem as a national one. It is the privilege of every citizen of this country to be either a regionalist or a provincialist or a federalist; but, above all, he has the duty of being a Canadian, and a Canadian before anything else. If individuals are not allowed to act, if their actions are prejudicial to and against the interest of the community, no prime minister, no government, no political party leader has the right to seek his own advantage or even the advantage of his province if his actions are detrimental to the country as a whole. I sincerely hope that if a dominion-provincial conference is
Industrial Relations

called our governments will approach the problem with this principle in mind. Should some provincial premier or other government leader act otherwise, he may gain a temporary political success, but sooner or later his own people will reproach him for having lost sight of the general welfare and interest of his country.
Mr. LIGUORI LACOMBE (Laval-Two
Mountains) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, I shall keep the length of my remarks within the strictest 'bounds, because this session has lasted but too long.
Speeches can never 'bring, strikes to an end. Only an energetic government, able to do justice to employees and, employers, can stop disputes. Let the, government, after such lengthy discussion, at last find the means of settling the strikes which paralyse the economy of this nation. The workers are justified in demanding a salary commensurate with the increase in the cost of living,. Employers cannot be unaware of what it costs to-day to live. I should rather say to subsist, because I leave out of consideration any luxury, and even reasonable comfort.
If employers are aware of that situation, the government are still better acquainted with it. They should decide on a course of action with the determination that the present circumstances require.
There have been enough words; the need is for action. No one can be made to believe that there are no grounds for understanding, no middle course that would put an end to these disastrous strikes which deeply affect the whole population. There should be no attempt to shirk responsibilities and shift them upon others. The established authority has the duty to safeguard the well-being of the people. Its duty is to do justice to all and with the least possible delay. The more we have discussions, conferences and speeches, the more difficult the situation will become.
In concluding my brief remarks, I shall remind the government that the Canadian people expect them to find a prompt, energetic, fair and efficient solution of the labour and industrial problem. Idle discussions will settle nothing.
We have no need of a national labour code. Each province has its own legislation on labour and industrial matters and they have jurisdiction to legislate thereon. Owing to the war and to this transition period, the dominion government has exercised, and still exercises, prerogatives reserved to the provinces. It would be useless to call a dominion-
.Mr. Langlois.]
provincial conference for the purpose of discussing the advisability of enacting a national labour code. As I have said not long ago, Canada and the world are being killed with conferences and speeches. The truth of this statement is evidenced by this unrestrained verbiage which should be replaced by action. And what can be said about the series of amendments moved a few minutes ago in connection with concurrence in the report of the committee, if not that it is systematic opposition and pure obstruction.
A committee of the house was appointed with instruction to inquire into the grievances of the employees and the claims of the employers. After weeks of discussion and investigation that committee can still, like ourselves, notice the same conflicts between capital and labour. Strikes are becoming more and more numerous, while members of Parliament are holding forth at a daily cost of $35,000 to the public treasury. Economists, or at least those who pretend to be economists, talk and talk without the slightest regard for economy. Their greatest concern is publicity and political propaganda. But neither the workers nor the people of this country can afford to wait. The government can and must end strikes through fair, energetic and immediate action. They are able to do justice to all the parties to the dispute and free this country from those woeful conflicts between capital and labour.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
When the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) was speaking the other day he read to the house a dispatch credited to the Canadian Press which told us that the picket lines at Hamilton had been opened, and that at least ten cars laden with men had gone into the plant. That statement was greeted with some jubilation in certain parts of this chamber. Perhaps those who applauded thought the picket lines had been definitely broken. Perhaps they believed the strike was over. But I say to this house if the strike is finished by smashing the union at Hamilton, then we are only on the verge of labour troubles unprecedented in Canada, and that is not a prophecy which will be very far wrong. Last April, when the increase of $5 a ton was granted to the manufacturers, labour was led to believe that in the $5 there was a certain amount for an increase in wages. The government would not tell the union how much was appropriated for wages; yet, as I say, the workers were led to believe that an amount w-as there. Because the government refused to tell the workers, we said then the government was sowing the seeds of

Industrial Relations
a labour war in Canada, and1 in. effect that is what is happening. The government cannot shuffle away from the responsibility it has in this matter.
In committee on industrial relations I imagine many hon. members learned much. They learned, for instance, that organized labour in Canada, as in most other countries, has had to fight for its very existence. Unions have had to fight to be born, and once they were created, frequently they were smashed and destroyed either by recalcitrant employers, or by the actions of agents provocateurs, or perhaps by the very apathy of the workers themselves. But it would be a great mistake to believe that trade unions are not here to stay. Unfortunately some employers seem to be of that opinion. They remind me of King Canute trying to hold back the waves of the sea. Organized labour has grown tremendously in strength in the last ten years. It will continue to grow; but, as things are now, it can only grow because it fights. We are told that organized labour is militant. Of course it is. It has had to be militant because it is faced with an equal militancy on the part of employers, who in all too many cases are determined to smash the unions. That, I think, is borne out by the evidence which was submitted to the committee on industrial relations. I refer to page 3 of the brief of Mr. Hilton, who, as the house knows, is president of Steel Company of Canada. Before that committee this man said:
It is emphasized that the Steel Company of Canada has not been and is not opposed to collective bargaining nor is it opposed to the principle of trade unionism.
That was Mr. Hilton speaking out of one corner of his mouth. He was questioned by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), who asked:
I am a member of a trade union and have been since 1910, and it was never necessary in the company with which I worked, and it is not necessary in normal labour relations with organized trade unions, to get a court order to recognize the union. In a great many of the trade unions and companies that I know where there are labour relations it has not been necessary to get a court order, but in the company of which you are president the trade union was never recognized except by a court order or an order of the labour relations board? Is that correct ?
And Hilton said:
I think that is correct, yes.
That is the man who at one moment professes to believe in the principle of trade unions and the next minute admits he will not recognize them unless compelled to do
so by a court order. Then the hon. member for Vancouver East went on:
At your Canada works at Hamilton you had a board of conciliation under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act in 11945?
A. You are asking me that question?
Q. Yes?	.	,
A. Yes, I believe that is right.
Q. Did that board of conciliation make a unanimous recommendation for a form of union security ?
A. It made that recommendation. I cannot tell you from memory whether or not it was unanimous.
Q. Did you accept the findings of the board? We will deal later with the question whether or not it was unanimous. Did the company, or did you accept for the company, the findings of the board of conciliation?
A. If you mean did we grant so-called union security at the Canada works we did not.
This, despite the unanimous recommendation of the board of conciliation. Then the hon. member for Calgary West asked a question:
You do not object to a voluntary check-off, do you?
A. I do.
Pursuing the matter further, Mr. Hilton said:
We sign a contract for one year at a certain wage rate, the next year it is going to be more. If you concede a revocable check-off this year, next year it will be something more; and it all leads up to a closed shop, which I do not approve of either.
Well, Mr. Hilton has the right to decide what he approves, but I do not think he has any right in the face of that evidence, to try to tell the workers in his plant that he believes in collective bargaining and is not opposed to the principles of trade unionism. It is true that to-day the dispute is over the question of an increase of fifteen cents, but fundamentally that fifteen cents is superficial to labour unrest in Canada. What we are in effect seeing, indeed what we are seeing, is the constant conflict we have had for so long between labour and capital as to who shall get what share of that which is produced. That is the fundamental aspect of the conflict before us to-day, and it is not one that will be resolved easily. Mr. Gordon, who appeared before the committee, had some ideas on the matter. At page 329 of the proceedings he was asked:
Now, it was quite evident that there was a certain amount in that $5 which had been allocated for wages.
His reply was:
No, not necessarily; that is the point I have been labouring to put forward. That was dependent entirely on the decision of the management of the steel company as to what profit level they were willing to operate on; and they could quite easily and quite reasonably have taken the attitude that they could not afford
Industrial Relations

to pay anything for wages because they were not earning a profit amount anywhere near the amount which they ought to ibe earning by prewar standards in relation to the volume of production that they are now undertaking.
There we see the orthodox, conventional defence of the capitalist system. Mr. Gordon says management will decide what profit level they are willing to operate on. We admit that steel is a basic industry, that it is a vital industry. We admit that our economy will collapse unless we get steel; yet steel will be produced only when the operators themselves decide that they are going to produce it. That is a position of utter social irresponsibility, the sort of position we in this party have constantly condemned both in this house and outside it. To-day private enterprise has no sense. of responsibility at all to the community as a whole. It is concerned only with the making and the maintenance of its own profit position.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: I suppose there are no decent people at all running industry in this country?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
There are quite a number of decent people running industry. Because a man believes in the capitalist form of economy is no reason for believing he is not decent. At times I believe the hon. gentleman himself is quite decent. May I repeat part of the same statement by Mr. Gordon:
. . . they were not earning a profit amount anywhere near the amount which they ought to be earning by pre-war standards in relation to the volume of production that they are now undertaking.
Here, surely, is a new gauge by which profits should be measured. During the war, in many cases, under the excess profits tax, the government decided that the capital invested was to be the gauge by which we would decide what profit should be paid. Now Mr. Gordon tells us it is his view-I do not say it is the government's view-that profits must have some relation to the entire productivity of the plant. In StelcO' there has been no increase in subscribed capital during the last few years; yet we are told that production is two and one-half times pre-war value. Surely, then, if production has been increased so much, and capital has remained as it was, the workers in the plant, those who are the producers, deserve a greater share of what has been produced.
Mr. Gordon apparently disagrees with that, but we in the C.C.F. would say that ours is the correct position to take. For too long those who have been- producing the essential needs in Canada have been exploited in precisely the same way, and capital has always been given the preferred position over human

beings. In effect, it boils down to this, that so far as those who are defenders of free enterprise are concerned-so. far as anybody is concerned; so far as economy is concerned, in industry-the owner lends his capital, but the industrial worker gives his life. There is that great difference, and the worker is not unduly reimbursed for what he gives. He starts in industry at an early age and, normally, if his health permits, he will carry through until he reaches the age of seventy, when he gets an old age pension. At times he may be laid off owing to unemployment. He may get two weeks holiday with pay, and very often without pay.
But the average worker in Canada cannot afford to stop work because, on account of the low wages he has been paid, he has no security. I mentioned in the house a few weeks ago that ndnetv-two per cent of workers in Canada who reached the age of sixty-five are penniless. And when we remember what their average wage is, we need not be surprised at that. After a man has brought up a family, clothed them, fed them, educated them, paid all the thousand and one expenses connected with raising a family, he will have very little left of his meagre earnings. Even if he got $33.60 a week he would have very little to put by for old age.
I would also say that it would be a mistake to assume that industry is the only sinner. Here is a case in point I should like to bring to the attention of the house, and particularly to the attention of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier). It casts a light over what I am saying. Here was a man employed by the government from 1896 to 1946. a man with excellent references. His employment as a labourer started at $1.50 a day, and gradually increased to $4. His wife is dead; he is a widower, and maintains in his home an invalid daughter. This year, when he had reached the age of seventy-nine, the government dispensed with his services, and in recognition of his fifty years in the department reimbursed him with a pension of $19.91 a month.
How can we expect industry to be any better than the government which sets an example like that, for the people of Canada? Organized workers in Canada do not want too much. All they want is some security, which is surely the right of every citizen. They want a 40-hour week, with no reduction in "take-home pay."
May I say to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) that the price ceiling is being shot rapidly. I have just had word from British Columbia that to-day the regional war labour board out there approved1 a 15-cent increase

Industrial Relations
in wages and a 40-hour week for the American Can Company. Things must be very dangerous for the price ceiling on the west coast, especially in view of the fact that perhaps the Dominion Bridge Company and Heaps Engineering will also get the same award.

speechtext: The hon. member said that the price control was being broken. I think he meant wage control.

No;
I said "price", because if fifteen cents here will pierce the price ceiling, I am sure fifteen cents in British Columbia would. If we are to have that pattern there I think we should have it here.
The unions favour the 40-hour week with no reduction in "take-home pay", but they do not make that request from every industry. Organized labour is willing to modify its demands according to the ability of an industry to pay. But it is not going to take the unvouched word of the companies as to how much they are earning, and in that respect I do not blame them. The workers are asking, so far as union security is concerned, for the union shop and the check-off. The workers also ask -and I am sure the acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) knows this-for the maintenance of price control in Canada.
I should like to quote at this point something Mr. Gordon said. Although he corrected the interpretation later, nevertheless the idea *has gone out that this only is what he said.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: My hon. friend has said that price control was blown to bits, and now he says he is asking for the maintenance of it.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
I said the workers are asking for price control, and I said the government is blowing it to bits, despite the fact that the workers are asking for it. Just ask the worker who will shortly be required to pay three cents a quart more for milk, and see what he thinks about the price ceiling.
Mr. Gordon said, at page 295:
Any increase in cost is inflationary, as I said; inflationary in the sense that in increasing the cost you must increase the price.
That does not necessarily follow, and Mr. Gordon pointed it out later. Increases in cost can be absorbed in two ways, either by taking them out of profits or by increasing production. And that increased production in Canada is not going to take place unless we get the workers back to work again; yet the policy of the government to-day is designed to bring about that very inflation which it seems to fear.
Mr. Gordon made a further significant statement-and I am sorry to be picking on him
all the time, but he is responsible for these statements and also for the apparent attitude which the government is taking. He was asked these questions and gave these answers:
Q. Let us be clear about this; you indicated a little while ago that if certain things happened, if certain increases are allowed, there would be no use trying to continue the system of control of prices, that at a certain point you might just as well close up was about the way you expressed it. Was that right?
A. That is correct.
Q. All right, Mr. Gordon; where is that point? Do you know?
A. I do not know where that point is.
This merely substantiates the point made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the leader of this group, when he said there was nothing scientific in the principle of ten cents being the point above which we would get a complete smash in the economy. As Pat Conroy said, Donald Gordon was working on a hunch. I think anybody else's hunch is just as good as that of Donald Gordon, the man who is in charge of the wartime prices board in Canada.
There are certain other factors which the government must face. One of the most important is the suspicion, inbred and ingrained, on the part of the worker, as to the good faith of the government and of employers. In other words, the worker feels he will not get justice. Last night the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) referred to certain alleged violations of the law which had taken place in Hamilton. He pointed out that those now working are being paid for twenty-four hours a day, that there is a landing strip for aircraft in the plant, that employees are staying and living in the plant. And again-and this was not refuted-he said that rationed goods are going into that plant in great quantities. I am not saying that in every case the law is being broken by Stelco, but I say in certain cases it is being broken by the company, and the government is taking no action against it.
The workers see other things. They see a union member punch a scab-and the minister, as an old union man, knows what a scab is-on the nose. The worker was sent down for sixty days. Then some other person comes along and fires a gun at members of the picket line and he is fined $10. There is no justice in that.
By and large, I think the minister has made good selections in his appointment of conciliation officers, but he did not make a good choice in the case of Mr. Justice Roach. To my mind, he was not impartial, and he said that the union was run by a dictatorship because the union would not accept some of his ideas. I should like to quote from the record
Industrial Relations

where Mr. Justice Roach is being questioned by the hon. member for Vancouver East as follows:
Q. On whose authority then did you, as commissioner, make this offer of ten cents across the board and the other matters associated with it?
A. I made it on my own responsibility.
Q. And if then you had no authority for this proposal, and if the men had accepted your suggestion, your proposal that this ten cents per hour wage increase should be put before the employees to be voted on by secret ballot and that secret ballot carried, what assurance did you have that the company would come through with the ten cents?
A. Oh, I had no assurance.
He expected the union to accept this hypothetical offer and then have another vote, and he was surprised because the union did not do so. Then he incorporated in his report the absolutely stupid statement that the union was working under a dictatorship.
There are one or two other points I should like to comment upon. Two or three days ago everybody was full of praise for the work of this committee, but now we are not so sure about it. I have no doubt that the members of the committee worked earnestly, assiduously and honestly, but to the great disappointment of the people of this country; they started out like a 16-inch howitzer and finished up like a pea-shooter.
There are two parts of the report with which I disagree. I do not like recommendation No. 5, which concerns itself solely with the law of picketing. If we are to concern ourselves with the law of picketing, there should also be a law on the statute books of this country about strike-breaking. Then in connection with recommendation No. 6 I find myself in substantial agreement with the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). As I interpret that recommendation, it means that after a strike vote has been properly taken at Stelco the minister is given permission to go and take another vote. If that is correct, then it is a violation of the rights of trade unions in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended taking part in this debate, but everybody else seems to be taking a little crack at something or other. Ever since this industrial relations committee was first set up, a number of thoughts have been going through my mind. I must confess that I was a little disappointed this afternoon that neither of the amendments proposed earlier in the day were permitted to go through. The committee started out with a fairly big job to do and I wanted to see it done right. I am not saying that no ground was covered by the committee, but I do say that during the past weeks they do not appear to have solved the problem. It seems to me that the mountain has laboured and brought forth a mouse.
I must confess that I never did hold out very much hope that a parliamentary committee would solve the problem. I am quite certain that no information was brought out during the sittings of that committee that the government did not have already, or that they could not easily have obtained if they wanted it. The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) seems to be the gentleman who conceived the idea that a parliamentary committee would be able to solve the problem and he rose in his place and made the suggestion to the government. Immediately the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) rose and said, "I am quite happy to accept the suggestion of my hon. friend." The hon. member for Calgary West has not been sitting in this house quite as long as some of us, and I want to say to him that I always am a little suspicious when the Prime Minister accepts a suggestion made by the opposition. Let me tell the hon. member for Calgary West this one-thing, that the Prime Minister has all the answers. Don't ever underrate his political acumen.

Clever,

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
I want to read from an article which appeared in 1943 in the Wholesale Grocers' News. It contains a statement made by Mr. William Green, president of the American Federation of Labor. This is what he said:
As the spokesman for a labour organization with six and a half million members, I want to make it emphatically clear here and now that the American Federation of Labor stands four-square in support of free and private enterprise. We recognize the right to own and manage property for public and private profit . . . We . . . will oppose any attempt to abridge, restrict or interfere with the functions of free enterprise . . .
Individual liberty and security are inseparably associated with the vital principle of free enterprise and the private ownership of property. These priceless blessings will remain with us only so long as we maintain the source from which they flow. They will go with the wind, pass beyond our reach and it will be difficult, if not impossible, to regain them if ever there is substituted for them any form of communism or governmental regimentation.
Because labour understands fully that it will suffer most if ever the foundation and superstructure of free government is destroyed or impaired, it stands firm in its determination to protect and preserve free enterprise and the private ownership of property at any cost.
Regardless of how capital and labour, employer and employee, management and workers, may disagree upon other economic, social and political questions, they stand united in defense of the maintenance of free enterprise and the preservation of the joint benefits which flow therefrom.
These are the words of William Green, president of the American Federation of Labor. I see that it is nearly six o'clock. I have something else to put on the record, but I realize that time is going, and I will conclude my remarks by repeating once again that ini the final analysis it must be the government's responsibility to solve the problems of the country. They should so legislate that those problems will not arise; but if they arise, they will be easy of solution. Any party which bids for power must be willing to accept that responsibility.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
In rising to continue the debate on the report of the industrial relations committee, I wish first to pay a tribute to the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) who spoke just before the recess. He always brings freshness, humour and a lot of common sense to our deliberations and we appreciate hearing him at any time.
I wish to endorse the statements which have been made by my colleagues who are members of the committee and other hon. members of the committee with regard to the way the committee worked. I should also like to pay tribute to the splendid work of the chairman and the general feeling of trying to do something to cure the industrial unrest in the country. We went to the committee meetings with a certain amount of suspicion, thinking that, possibly, the members of the various political parties would try to jockey for position. In the first few days that was perhaps a little apparent, but it soon died out because we got to know each other much better.
There were members on the committee who were new members of the house; and when the committee finally reached the in-camera stage to bring in its report there was a feeling amongst all the members-even though three of them did oppose one section of the report- that they had tried to do a good job and had worked long and arduous hours in doing so.
Now that the report has come into the house for endorsation, we find that many members who were not on the committee are condemning it because it did not settle the strikes which are prevalent throughout Canada. Throughout the proceedings of the committee I contended-and I was supported generally by most members of the committee-that our job was not to settle the prevailing strikes but to try to evolve some machinery as an improvement on the present machinery so that we could avoid strikes in the future.
I do not think any member of the committee went to its meetings, and I do not think the members of the house thought that they would go there with the idea that they were going to set the standard of wages, the hours of labour or other conditions for which unions and industry are struggling. I do not think it was our job to do that, but out of the committee has come a report which, if implemented by the government, will, in my opinion, do a great deal to cure the ills from which industry is suffering.
In fighting political battles I have never been one who has pulled my punches. When
Industrial Relations

I go out to fight a political battle I put everything I have into it, but I have never yet used personalities in any election campaign in which I have participated. I resent hon. members rising in their places and asking for the head of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). When election time comes round I shall go out and try to defeat the Minister of Labour, not because he is Minister of Labour, but because he is following the philosophy of a party with which I disagree. I suppose I have known the Minister of Labour longer than any other member of the House of Commons. In fact, back in the old days he and I belonged to the same party. In those days we were fairly successful in that party. I have known him for many years and I have had a high regard for him as a man who knew labour, but he was a conservative, careful labour leader.
I remember one Saturday morning going home from Ottawa. I usually drop into a little hotel in Toronto for my breakfast because I have to stay over there. I met my friend Humphrey. Humphrey was on his way to fight a by-election in Welland after having been named Minister of Labour. I shook hands with him and congratulated him on having been named Minister of Labour. I said to him then: "Humphrey, if you are permitted to handle the Department of Labour without any political interference"- and I do not mean narrow political interference; I mean the general policy of the government-"if you are allowed to do that, I have no fear whatever 'but that you are going to make a real success of a very difficult job." But he is in this position. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) says, "I want more money." He provides for it in his budget and we pay or else. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Claxton) says, "These are the regulations under which you will take this or that medicine; these are the regulations under which you must work." The Minister of Labour is dealing with human beings. He is dealing with men who are not always easy to deal with. I say this quite frankly and - sincerely, that many of the things which he could do and would do, many of "the things which he has tried to do-and I am not giving any special praise to him-have been nullified because of the very thing which my colleague, the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) referred to, namely, the lack of liaison, the lack of cooperation between the various departments of government. What better example have we than what is happening to-day?
A few weeks ago the government announced that they were going to remove the subsidy on

milk. What did that mean? It meant a two-cent increase in the price of a quart of milk to the consumers of the country. The government said that this will save $20 or $22 million a year. If it were a saving and it were shown in the budget, or in the expenditures for the coming year as a saving, then we could readily say that we were going back to the normal peace-time type of business. They removed the subsidy, and the burden which used to be put on the treasury of Canada is now placed on the shoulders of the people, particularly the fathers of large families who have to buy the milk. At the same time we pick up the supplementary estimates and find millions of dollars for public buildings. Surely, when we need houses for our people, when we are trying to hold the line on inflation, when we wish to see to it that we shall not have the conditions which followed after the last war-and I went through them-at least we ought to see to it that we protect the line in every department of government. What has happened? We hear now that the producer subsidy on milk is to be taken off. In Ottawa this will mean that milk which, under the previous subsidies, cost the consumer ten cents a quart will now cost fifteen cents a quart, or an increase of fifty per cent. Then the industrial worker will come to the Minister of Labour and say, "I must have more wages. I cannot feed my family, because with the increased cost of all these things my children must have I am not getting enough money." ' Those are the problems with which the minister is faced. So that I say I am not one of those who will go out and demand the head of the Minister of Labour. I am quite prepared, when an election comes around, to go out and ask for the heads of everybody sitting over there, but I do say that we should at least be fair about these things.
To-night I wish to deal with this problem in perhaps a little different way from that in which other speakers have dealt with it. As I say, I do not think our committee was set up for the purpose of establishing wages, hours and so on. We were set up to try to evolve some better machinery, and if this report is implemented by the government it will at least be something. But let us go back over the years since the beginning of the war. When war broke out, a great many industrialists in this country realized that the cost of living had increased, and. they raised wages. Others did not. Then came the law providing for the cost of living bonus. This was all based on 1939 figures. Were they the right ones? I do not know; I would say not. I would say that the wage rate of 1939

Industrial Relations
was not a fair rate, because of conditions that existed at that time; and certainly the cost of living, taken in those terms, was not comparable. However, that was what the government did. Then, after a time during which industry was supposed to pay this cost of living bonus, wages were frozen. What had happened? A great many industries in this country had not been paying the cost of living bonus, with the result that, when, wages were frozen, under the law they could not pay the bonus which previously they had denied to their employees. So that we had in the cities and towns across Canada a checker-board system of wages which certainly was unfair to the industrial workers. Later, we had tremendous taxation imposed upon the wages of those workers, taxation which year after year caused loss of production and absenteeism. Why? Our people have become educated in the last few years. They have had to make out income tax returns, and now they know how to use figures. If you asked a man to work on Saturday afternoon he would figure that if he worked four hours his earnings for that week would be so increased that he would have to work those four hours for seventeen or eighteen or nineteen cents; and the higher his rate of pay, the less he actually received for working overtime.
The whole scheme was such that the financial policy of the government was nullifying the very thing the price control board and the Minister of Labour were trying to do. Time after time in budget debates we asked this government to grant greater exemptions to industrial workers. They refused. They were taxing the people of this country, so they said, not only to get revenue but to stop inflation. One budget came down and provided for compulsory savings. This was to give the workers of this country a backlog of savings with the government for the time when the W'ar wrould be over and we would be going through the reconstruction period. The following year, after protests from all across the country because of the money that was being taken from the pay envelopes of the workers, in his budget the Minister of Finance said they were going to relieve the people of these compulsory savings. They were not giving the industrial workers of the country anything. They were just letting them keep the money which was rightfully theirs. At that time we urged, "If you want to stop inflation, increase the exemptions of the industrial workers. Put them under a compulsory savings plan if you wish, but at least they will know that when the war is over and they go through a period which may mean unem-63260-329
ployment for a time they will have this money as a backlog to look after themselves and their families." Another budget came down. Again we urged increased exemptions in the lower income brackets. Again it was refused. I say this, and it is not being said in a critical sense but because I want to point out to the members of this house that much of our labour discord, many of the problems with which the Minister of Labour is faced to-day, are not due to the way in which the Department of Labour has tried to administer the law but to the general policy of the government, which I think was unfair to the industrial workers of Canada. If this government had brought down a 1946 budget in 1946, instead of bringing down a 1947 budget in 1946, at least the industrial workers would have been given some slight relief.
There is the whole question with which we are faced. Coming as I do from an industrial riding, I have some knowledge of industrial workers. Some of my hon. friends to my left, as I said this afternoon, would condemn every manufacturer in Canada by saying they are not honest; they cannot be trusted; they have not the interests of their employees at heart. That is the sort of stuff that starts communism in any country. Those are the kind of speeches that stir up unrest. I went to work; I punched the clock at twenty minutes after six o'clock in the morning -when I first started, and I was given pretty small pay; even the employer thought he was paying me too little. But these hon. gentlemen, as the hon. member for Macleod said this afternoon, think they are the only ones who represent labour. All I could see in their whole scheme was the politics behind it all. How well do I remember that in various elections certain union leaders went out and told their followers. "This is how you vote. You vote for the C.C.F." These people talk about their love of labour and what they will do for labour, but they are ready and willing to have union leaders regiment the most sacred thing a man has; that is, his ballot. They are prepared to let those leaders turn those ballots their way, in order to "put a socialist flag on capital hill", as they decided at their annual meeting in Saskatchewan the other day they would like to do.
