speechtext: Tell some of that to Mr. Hilton.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Hilton handled himself very well before the committee. And I did not see any of your men doing anything to subscribe to what your leader, and other members who were not on the committee, suggested should be done.

Industrial Relations

Let me say this, that I am surprised at what the leader of the C.C.F. said yesterday, that he is willing to tie wages to profits. Let him ask any union leader in this country if he is prepared to have the wages of his union members tied to the profits of a company. Furthermore, he said he was also prepared to advocate that personal productivity should be the extent of wages a man should earn-personal productivity. If you do not believe it, look up the records of Hansard, because I asked him the question.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext: It should be a factor.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
I asked him the question. I say these are the men who presume to represent labour; and yet, as the hon. member for Macleod said, how many of them represent industrial ridings in the Dominion of Canada to-day? The point I was coming to was this, that one thing I could see in that committee, as a result of the briefs placed there by the union, a thing which I know is bothering a lot of people back home, a thing which I know is bothering industrial workers in this country, is the fear of the future. It is a real, live fear, because the last depression is so close to us. I do not blame them for that fear. Therefore I say that if we had the type of liaison and the type of cooperation between various departments of government that I think there ought to be, many of these difficulties would be solved, and much of the legislation which passes one department and is negatived by another would disappear.
What do we find? Hon. members in this house, and particularly those in the C.C.F., find fault that we have not come in with certain specific recommendations. Let me say that two members of the C.C.F. party who sat on that committee endorsed its policy, all the way through the picture. They endorsed the report; they endorsed clause 6. And what was clause 6? Clause 6 gives the right to the working man to declare what tie wants, by secret ballot. I am not going to deny him that right. If we are going to deny the working man that right, then we might as well have regimentation immediately. It is a right they have. If what many of the men who are out on strike to-day say is true, if many men, with whom I have been associated for years and who are active in labour circles had had the secret ballot; if there had been no intimidation, and if they had all had an opportunity to vote, those plants would be producing to-day, as they ought to be.
This afternoon the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) took my colleague the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) to task because he referred to communism, and

because he referred to communists who were heading some of the unions in this country. Let there be no mistake; there never was a more perfect plan to communize Canada than there is at work .to-day. We have seen it in the last few years. Strangers come into town and stir up industrial friction, organize a few men into a union and call the factory on strike, without any hope of winning the strike. But they do it for one purpose: They do it because they want to cause unrest. They want to thwart authority. They do not want these strikes to be settled; they do not want peace in industry. They want to create unrest, and to sabotage the whole economy of Canada. Just as soon as these men see that there is no chance of winning the strike- and I have seen it time and again; I know the Minister of Labour has seen it-they get out from under, sneak away and leave these strikers, whom they have urged to go out, holding the bag.
What is behind this plan, this well-conceived plan, a plan which they must have never expected to bring into actuality? They do this because they can sneak away and leave 100, 150, 200 or 250 strikers that they have taken out of industry, and most of whom want to work-they leave those workers holding the bag, in the belief that they have left behind at least twenty-five or thirty, or perhaps a few more, communists.
They are men with hatred in their hearts, men who hate their employers, men who hate constituted authority, men who hate everything. And why? Because they are led by these men, led to go out on strike. If they can carry out that pattern in every industrial centre in Canada, as they are trying to do, Tim Buck will have his 40,000 communists in this country.
Mr. Speaker, this is a serious situation. I find fault with the government for having passed an order in council and then not enforcing it. Our committee report says that law is the basis of society. Undoubtedly, after the most careful consideration the government passed an order in council. That order in council provided that a controller would be put into the steel company plants. The order in council provided that those who violated it wTould be punished; there was a punishment clause inserted. It provided that, the steel controller having taken over the plants, having taken the plants from these companies, they were no longer the property of those companies, but rather the property of the government of Canada. The steel controller had power to make agreements as to wages or anything else.
Why did he not exercise those powers? Why is the government going to allow lawlessness

Industrial Relations
in this country? If we allow that, then goodness knows what will happen in the very near future. If we are to overlook the breaking of law, as it has been done in Hamilton-and I do not care whether it is industry or the employee who breaks it-and as it was done in Windsor, then surely we cannot blink at things like that. But we have done it.
Some members will say to me that under an order in council you could take these men into court and fine them for a breach of the order in council. They would say, "If you were Minister of Labour or Minister of Justice would you be prepared to drag 2,400 or 2,500 people into court and fine them for breach of the law?" My answer would be this, that if I were not prepared to carry out the order in council I would not have passed it.
I have said that when the committee met we got to know each other better. I feel that the members of the committee sat dowrn with the honest intention of accomplishing something. We now come into the house and we find that there is certain opposition to the report.
I am not surprised at the attitude of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Mac-Innis) toward matters pertaining to labour, toward matters pertaining to the general economy of the country, and toward industry in this country. I have never heard him say anything good about industry in this country and I do not expect he ever will. There are certain people w'ho can continue with that attitude and that type of feeling in their ridings and perhaps the people will continue to return them to the House of Commons. As I say, I was not surprised at the attitude of the hon. member for Vancouver East, because to him anyone who employs anyone is just taboo. He wants to have no association with such a man. When the hon. member was speaking in the house on November 6, 1945, the hon. member for London (Mr. Manross) asked a couple of questions. I quote from page 1894 of Hansard as follows:
Mr. Manross:	How many men did you ever
hire?
Mr. Maclnnis:	I never hired anybody.
Mr. Manross:	And never will.
Mr. Maclnnis:	Quite right, and I do not
want to because I do not want to make a living by exploiting somebody else.
That is the policy of one of the chief lieutenants of the leader of the C.C.F. Supposing every one who started any type of industry in this country had had the same idea? There would not have been any industry in Canada; there would not have been anything in this country. Some of those hon. members condemned communism in the committee, and I believe they were sincere; but speeches such 63260-3291
as we have heard during this debate will certainly do nothing to bring industrial peace to this country. Rather they will do everything to stir up industrial unrest.
I do not happen1 to be one of those who can look back to centuries of British blood behind him; I happen to be a descendant of people who came from Europe, a long time ago it is true. They came here, and all they asked was the right to set their feet on the shores of Canada and be permitted to work out their destiny. They could not speak English when they came here, but that is 140 years ago. They saw what was happening in their own fatherland and they left, not because they hated their fatherland but because they loved freedom more. They came to Canada, and over the years like hundreds of thousands of others they struggled to make this country what it is to-day. They asked for no favours; all they asked was the right to work, to live their own lives and to raise their children with a certain amount of freedom to them.
They never thought the day would come when this land of their adoption would be faced with the very thing that they had hated over there, with the very thing that was the curse of Europe, the thing that will be the curse of Canada unless we take steps now to see that it is wiped and blotted out. I blame the government for not enforcing the law as they ought to. I blame the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) for having written to the city council of Hamilton saying, "While this committee is sitting, I am not prepared to say what I would do with regard to enforcing the law." I do not know that you should have the right to suspend a law simply because the House of Commons is sitting. Supposing we had been discussing capital punishment or thievery or something else, would you have suspended the laws because some committee was discussing those matters?
This thing is so serious that it will take a strong hand to handle it. We have a wonderful future, a future for which thousands and thousands of men died in this war and thousands and thousands died in the first great war. It is up to us to see to it that the future they fought to preserve for us is preserved. The only way we can do this is by seeing to it that the law in Canada is lived up to and that communism, with all the viciousness that it represents, is wiped out.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I
should like to compliment the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homiuth) upon his remarks, because they take me back to the old days. His views on government and the rights of labour, notwithstanding the fact
Industrial Relations

that he sits there and I stand here, have not differed since those days. I agree with him on the broad question of freedom; I believe in what is sometimes called free enterprise.
I often wonder what would have happened to the freedom of some of my hon. friends during the recent war had it not been for this vicious system of free enterprise they speak of. Over fifty per cent of the industrial production of the world is to be found in North America. Had it not been for that tremendous industrial machine and the will to die if necessary to save a way of life on the part of the young men in our fighting forces, freedom as we understand it would have perished from the earth.
Let me say to my hon. friends who believe in the philosophy of communism, if you can call it a philosophy, that had it not been for the driving forces of our free institutions, communism as they understand it might have perished from the face of the earth and fascism might have reigned supreme upon the continent of Europe. Let us be frank and honest about this and give credit where credit is due.
The driving force of free enterprise, of the people who at one time stood alone to save free institutions as we understand them, was what saved our civilization. In my judgment, some of the so-called leaders in this country have deliberately set in motion policies designed to destroy the reconversion efforts of the Canadian people. Where were those so-called leaders prior to the entry of Russia into the war? Let us look at the record.

I have no objection to interruptions because I have lived in that atmosphere all my life. I come from a town where we glory in it. What I wanted to bring to the attention of the house is this: You cannot play politics at this particular time with the destiny of a nation. I am sure that my hon. friend the member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) after being here for a couple of sessions must sometimes like myself wish

he had stayed at home to enjoy the balmy breezes of the foothills of the Rockies. I know I sometimes regret being in my present position, but like my hon. friend I felt it my duty, during the difficult period we have been passing through in the last six years, to stay on. Let me compliment him upon making the motion he did and upon the statesmanlike attitude he took on the broad question of industrial relations when he made his speech in the House of Commons. I do not say this to flatter him but he showed deep insight into the processes that have made our democratic institutions what they are, and a deep insight also into the aims and aspirations of the working people of this country. I want to point out that the motion to establish the committee was supported by every member of this House of Commons without exception. The report of the committee was a unanimous one, with the exception that two members of the committee disagreed with one section of the report.

speechtext:
Well, then, history has been made. I did not see much of my hon. friend in the committee but he must have come along later. I believe that the committee rendered a distinct service. The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell), in the course of his address, asked me if I had learned anything from the committee. I am certain that the people of Canada learned something from the discussions in the committee for, after all, the processes of democratic government breathe and live on difficulties such as were presented to us. We had officers of labour organizations and of industry appear before the committee and give their opinions on labour conditions as they are at this moment. I do not think any member of the committee felt that a conciliation board of thirty-five members could settle any industrial dispute. The committee was not set up for that purpose, and the record will bear me out in that statement. I think it was the hon. member for Calgary West who suggested that we endeavour to settle the dispute in the steel industry, and Mr. L. W. Brockington, K.C., was asked to assume that onerous duty. I want to pay this tribute to Mr. Brockington: I think he served the committee well.
May I add that Mr. Justice W. D. Roach also served the committee well. At the very basis of our institutions is the right to differ in opinion, and it may be that some differed with the opinions of Mr. Justice Roach, but

Industrial Relations
undoubtedly he has rendered a distinct service both to labour and to employers by acting as chairman of fourteen or fifteen conciliation boards, and he assumed the difficult position of commissioner in this dispute in the light of his previous experience.
The speeches that have been made in this house since the committee's report has been before us have given some indication of the difficulties in industrial disputes. I have had some experience in these matters, and I do not believe that you can settle an industrial dispute by making statements to the newspapers. Industrial disputes are not settled in that way. Nor can you, in my judgment, settle them by taking sides in this house. At this very moment conferences are going on in the largest industry in this country in connection with a dispute over wages. You see nothing about it in the newspapers; yet these conferences are going on in a constructive effort to effect a settlement.
I do not think you can be a trade union leader and a politician at the same time. I say that from practical experience. My Conservative friends, particularly my hon. friend the member for Haldiimand (Mr. Senn), will remember that it was a regular thing some years ago for the Conservatives to win Hamilton East. In fact we had to pick out the sacrificial goat to take a beating by our Conservative friends. But, thank heaven, those days are past.
Mr. SENN; There is another day coming.

In those days in Hamilton we used to call them the "latter day saints." As I say, I have always been a believer in higher wages and progressive legislation irrespective of whom it was introduced by. I still maintain that position to-day.
As I have said before in the house, we have an obligation to the millions of defenceless people in the country who cannot protect themselves. We have an obligation to see to it that, as far as humanly possible, with all the trials, tribulations, difficulties and pressures, we protect the living standards of that., as I call them, great defenceless mass of people in Canada. So far as I am concerned, while I have breath in my body I am going to continue to do just that very thing, notwithstanding what may be said by those people who, if they had their way would destroy to-morrow morning freedom as we understand it.
That brings me to another point, but I might stay with price stabilization a little longer. With regard to the present disputes, I think it can be freely admitted by all of us that in 1944 we established a labour code in this country under the jurisdiction of the Department of Labour. I give credit to every party in the house for not criticizing that code at that time, which is an indication that they approved it. It was endorsed by every labour organization in the country. For the first time in the history of Canada labour organizations were protected by law and given the right to
bargain collectively. I am frank to admit that the organizations played some part in it, but, since the establishment of that code, labour organizations in Canada have grown faster than at any time in their history. Let us give credit where credit is due.
Then in the Department of Labour we built up the largest conciliation service in the history of the department, a conciliation service which, in my judgment, given a degree of common sense by both sides and the will to conciliate, can solve any industrial dispute. But I do not think there is any substitution for common sense and conciliation in the adjudication of labour disputes, and that goes for both sides.
It was said by an hon. member here this afternoon, who claimed that he was a trade unionist, that we were out to destroy trade unions. Any man who would say that in this day and age-well, it is amazing to me that he should be a member of the House of Commons.

As I have said before, any employer who thinks he can destroy labour unions is just wasting his time. He might just as well try to push back the St. Lawrence river. As a son of a trade unionist and a trade unionist by conviction, I believe that there is no substitution for a well-organized, well-disciplined and well-run trade union as an instrument for the advancement of the working people of Canada.
May I stay with price controls for a moment longer. You cannot have it both ways. I shudder to think what would happen in this

nation to-morrow if we wiped out price control. Supposing we wiped out rent control. Let us go into the matter with our eyes wide open. What would happen if we wiped out rent control; who would be the greatest sufferers? I think everyone will agree that the working people of this country would be the sufferers. There are many other aspects of price control I could enumerate along those lines.
I now come to section 6, which everybody is bothered about. We are going into uncharted seas here, I am frank to admit, but I have always argued that if you have a good case you need never be afraid to go before any tribunal you think is reasonably honest and decent. Neither should anyone who has a good case be afraid to put it into a secret ballot box. That is so crystal clear to me. The hon. member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Archibald) have had a great deal of experience in these matters, I am sure, as I have; and they must have known cases where people were brought in from the street to vote in what did not in the least resemble a ballot as we understand it. The united mine workers of America, from their own practical experience, saw to it that such a condition should be part of the machinery of their organization. I have a vivid recollection-one of many-of a meeting of about sixty people who, by a show of hands, called a strike of 1,400 people. I do not think that is the proper way to run any kind of organization.
I could give the house many examples. I was chairman of a commission having to do with a dispute being run by one of the witnesses who appeared before the industrial relations committee, where they brought people in from the street to cast a strike ballot. And mind you, I think that cuts both ways. I have knowledge of employers doing the same thing, so that all the disciples are not on one side. I think, with a staff skilled in the application of this recommendation of the committee, any minister of labour can use the judgment which is necessary to see to it that it is carried out fairly. If he does not ne should not be minister of labour, and possibly would .not be after the next election. That is the great curative force in all these matters. I believe it is well worth giving a try. I am not going to suggest that it is a cure, you understand, Mr. Speaker, but let me remind hon. members that, with the exception of three members of the committee, this was a unanimous report, which is an indication of the drift of public opinion in regard to the irresponsible leadership of organizations. That is inevitable. The pendulum swings both ways. This is an indication of the feeling in 
the minds of the members of the committee, who represent a broad cross-section of the people of this dominion.
The question of picketing has been touched upon. I have not a great deal more to say about that than I said when I answered the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Mae-Innis) the other day. I am going to repeat my statement at that time. I think an Englishman's home is his castle. I believe he has a right to move from his home to his place of work or business and back again without being molested by anybody, whether they are in the employ of an employer or of a trade union. Let us walk down the middle of the road. I have known the day of the picket line. I have knowrn the day of the goon squad, a day which in this dominion I am happy to say is fast passing. The suggestion has been made that we study the law of picketing. The law of Canada in regard to picketing is akin tc. the law of Great Britain. I was a party to making submissions to Hon. Mr. Guthrie, who was then minister of justice, which brought about the amendment in 1934 of the law concerning picketing. If hon. members are keen on studying that I can tell them it was the submission of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada of April, 1934. I could read it, but it is quite a lengthy submission. I remember talking to Mr. Guthrie, who in those days sat where the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) now sits.

That is an encouragement. I think in five or ten minutes I can finish. Let me repeat; I do not think you can have price control without a measure of wage stabilization. We built up across this country a system of boards composed of representatives of labour and of industry, with an impartial chairman, and in some cases the Minister of Labour. Labour representation was put on those boards at the request of labour organizations. Here again, Mr. Speaker, even with the building up of that machinery and all the conciliation services, I do not know how one can settle any labour dispute unless both parties are prepared to use the machinery placed at their disposal. Let us go one step farther. The will of the majority should prevail. The vast majority of the trade unions of this country have availed themselves of the instrumentality of these respective boards. Here, however, you have men representing forty thousand people 'who deliberately set out to circumvent the boards established for that purpose.

Industrial Relations
We talk of industrial councils. I am all for them, but I do not believe in compulsory cooperation. I do not believe it is practical, logical or sensible. My advice to the steel workers, to the electrical workers, to the rubber workers and to all other trade unions, in their own selfish interest if you want to put it on that level, and my advice to the employers-and you can put that on the same level-in the interests of our way of life, is that they avail themselves of the machinery set up by the government for the adjudication of labour disputes in this country. Anyone who advises to the contrary is in my opinion, not rendering a service to the employers, the employees or the nation itself. That is why Mr. Brockington's task was so difficult. That is why Mr. Justice Roach's task was so difficult. That is why the task of anybody, in any dispute, is so difficult, when the two parties will not avail themselves of the machinery established by law in this country. My mind goes back to the last British general strike. I have a definite recollection of what led up to it, and what happened after it was finished. It was germinating for many months, and those of us who were there will remember it well. Mr. John Clynes, who was a minister in the war cabinet in the first great war, and secretary of one of the largest organizations in Great Britain had this to say:
I have no doubt that we shall be told that this new-found and ill-digested policy is worth a trial. Those who have thought this matter out know that in giving it a trial they would begin by paralysing our industries and our whole social system. That paralysis would affect first, and worst, the masses of the poorer population. You cannot do it without anticipating a condition of civil war.
I believe this sincerely, that our thoughts should not be influenced by sentiment. If these present disputes are to be considered as substitutes for legal processes, then it is a challenge to our form of government and to our way of life.
I shall not detain the house longer, except to say, as my hon. friends in the committee said, that there are people in this country who do not want us to succeed in our reconversion programme. They do not fit into the pattern of things. They are the people who call for the abolition of wage controls. They are the people who call for the resignation of myself and Donald Gordon, and everybody who attempts to express an opinion in this country. Mr. Speaker, if hon. members across the way are eager to get on with the work of the house they will help both themselves and the house by keeping quiet, because I do not intend to be shouted down. I will stay here as long as necessary.
I was about to say that the country generally and the labour movement in particular will be disappointed in the speech just made by the Minister of Labour. I am not saying that particularly to criticize the minister; I say it advisedly, because I feel the people of Canada at a critical time like this, when production is being held up by industrial unrest, and when the labour movement which to-day, I believe, is trying to cooperate with the government, is being pushed in the face, in return, would have expected that the Minister of Labour, after a long debate of this kind,

would rise in his place and place before the country .some plan, and seme solution for the present situation.
In spite of that, we heard nothing to-night that we have not heard in the last three days. And the Minister of Labour, instead of telling the house and country what he and his government intend to do to rectify the situation which exists in Hamilton-and it is a serious situation-spent his time in lecturing the house about communism, and things of that kind. Let me say at the outset that I hold no brief for communism, neither does the party with which I am associated. However, it is strange that in June of last year before the election we did not hear these inflammatory speeches against communism by our friends the Liberals because at that time it was more convenient to keep oS the subject.
What are the workers asking for to-day? They are not asking for much, only a living wage as was referred to by the speaker to my left. They are simply asking for something that will put them where they can keep their families and themselves in these post-war years. They are not even asking for more money than they were receiving; they are just asking for wages high enough to compensate for the higher cost of living. When they find it necessary to go out on strike to get this, what does the Minister of Labour do? He calls them communists.
I will admit that not all members of the Progressive Conservative party think in this way, but one member spent most of his time while he was speaking to-night, in tell us about the horrors of communism. I maintain that the time may come when it may be necessary to debate the virtues or otherwise of communism or any other ism, but this debate is not the time at which to do so. I believe that in this debate hon. members should have stuck to the question, and the question is: What are we going to do about the industrial unrest in Canada?
I think it is wrong to suggest to the people of this country that all our labour troubles are caused either by communists or by politicians. There must be a basic reason why people go out on strike. People do not go out on strike simply because they are well off; there must be a basic reason for this unrest and that reason has not been brought out. The hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) made a statement which I believe should be corrected. He referred to the speech of my leader who spoke earlier in this debate and he accused him of being in favour of tying wages to profits and a few other things. He was asked this question by

Industrial Relations
the hon. member for Waterloo South, and he made this reply as reported on page 5172 of Hansard of August 21:
Mr. Homuth:	Would the hon. member pay a
man according to his personal productivity?
Mr. Coldwell:	I would say that, taking an
industry on the whole, the average productivity of the individual in that industry should bear some relationship to the amount he receives in wages; in addition to the productivity per man, the profits of the industry, the reserves which have been built up by the industry, the working capital and other financial factors, and the relation of the particular industry to the economy as a whole, the standard of living and wages of the workers concerned, and all the factors . . .
That makes it quite clear that he was looking at the picture in its broad form. The reason why this group has been carrying on this debate is not the reason we have been accused of. It is not to make political capital; it is simply because we feel-I have good reason for feeling this myself-that the work of the committee has not been completed. I do not intend to say anything disparagingly about the work of the committee because I have great respect and admiration for the members of it. I attended a few meetings because I was interested in the proceedings, although I was not a member. I always found the committee members to be hard1 working, industrious men who were putting in a great deal of their time. But the work of the committee is not completed.
To support my contention, I should like to bring to the attention of the house what the president, of the Canadian federation of agriculture, Mr. H. H. Hannam, had to say in a letter dated August 14, which he addressed to the chairman of the committee. The letter reads:
Dear Sir,-
The report of hearings which your committee has conducted into industrial relations prompts us to suggest that there has been no assembling nor appraisal of facts and information on which the decisions of such a committee ought to rest. No doubt you and members of your committee feel this very keenly.
That is the opinion of the man who represents the organized farmers of this country. In his opinion the committee had not yet acquired the data and information on which it could form a conclusion. Further on, he makes a recommendation or suggestion, as follows;
We believe that the first step in facing up to this situation would be the appointment of a royal commission which would survey the division of the national income as indicated by the levels of farm prices, industrial wages and corporation profits, and make recommendations for adjustment of balance where necessary, and submit a charter of economic rights which would commend itself to the people generally, and 63260-330J
thereafter serve as the basis for necessary action in the preservation of industrial peace and the maintenance of an equitable economic balance among all groups.
When a man such as the president of the Canadian federation of agriculture expresses the opinion that the work of the committee was not finished; when we have members on practically all sides of the house admitting that, although the committee tried to get all the information they could, there was a great deal they could not get, then there is good reason for this group moving the amendment which was moved this afternoon to the effect that the whole question should be sent back to the committee to give them an opportunity to finish the job they started.
The work of the committee was not finished because, regardless of the technical terms of its reference, I believe it was understood by the people of this country that it was appointed in a time of crisis to try to bring to parliament a formula for the solution of industrial disputes, and that formula has not been presented. The recommendations in the report are not particularly harmful because they do not mean a great deal. They are recommendations which probably could have been put in any report. But they do not do the job which the committee set out to do. The situation in Hamilton has not improved and the number of strikes have not decreased. The intensity of the antagonisms that existed has not been lessened, and we find that to-day the country is faced with the same situation that existed on July 16.
I should like to refer to something which was given as the chief reason for the difficulty the committee had. An hon. member to my left asked me whether the controller had the right to settle a strike. Apparently that is one of the things the government overlooked in the order in council, giving the controller the authority to settle the strike, because section 10 says:
The commissioner, the Hon. Mr. Justice W. D. Roach will continue with his duties as an industrial disputes inquiry commission as aforesaid, and the bargaining representatives of the aforesaid employees and the companies-
Note, it says, "employees and the companies".
-shall continue their negotiations with a view to the settlement of the matters presently in
dispute between them and shall negotiate in good faith with one another and make every reasonable effort to conclude a settlement.
After giving the controller such wide powers over practically the opinions of the workers, I do not see why the government should not have given him power to negotiate with the workers. Then he might have been able to do what is provided in section 11 of the order in council, which says:
The controller is hereby authorized to apply on behalf of each of the said companies to the appropriate war labour boards for an immediate increase in the wage rates of employees employed at the aforesaid establishments of the said companies, and to give effect to any authorization or direction which may be made or issued by any such war labour board.
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Han-sell) stated this evening that, in spite of this long debate, no member of the house had presented a solution for the industrial unrest we now have in this country. I am not going to say that is altogether true, because there may have been suggestions here and there which the hon. member may have overlooked; but, generally speaking, his statement may be true. If the government wanted to solve the impasse which things seemed to have reached at Hamilton they might consider the taking over of the steel industry of Canada as a public-owned utility. Why do I say that? I know hon. members will say that it is because I am a socialist, but that is not altogether so. I am not one of those who would socialize for the sake of socialization. I am one of those who believe that where it is necessary to take over an industry or utility or service and run it under public ownership in order to make it serve the people, that should be done.
I think it is not accidental that the Polymer plant, which is a publicly-owned industry, has been singularly free from strikes. Research Enterprises, T.C.A., and a great many other publicly-owned organizations have been free from strikes for a number of years. There is something which we must face in the future; it is this. People talk about private enterprise for the sake of opposing it; but do not hon. members agree with me that in a highly industrialized and highly civilized country the point will come at which you cannot have national development and at the same time have economic empires within the nation, each trying to run their own show? There must come a point at which basic industries that have a great influence over the lives of the people will have to become public utilities. By that I do not mean that every industry has to become publicly-owned; but you cannot have economic empires, with men at the head
Industrial Relations

of them who are not concerned about public welfare but are concerned only with their profits-and I am not saying that that is immoral, either; it seems to be a natural outcome of our economic system-concerned only with the expansion and accumulation of wealth in their own hands, coming into contact, sometimes suddenly, with public opinion, coming into conflict with other economic empires, and creating chaos in this countiy. That cannot be. Why do I say that?
I have here somewhere a quotation which I should like to read to the house. I happen to to be an adherent of the Catholic religion, but that is not the main reason why I read this. This is a quotation from His Holiness the late Pope Pius XI, in his Quadragesimo Anno, in which he points this out:
It is rightfully contended that certain forms of property must be reserved to the state since they carry with them the opportunity for domination too great to be left in. the hands of private individuals without injury to the community at large.
I would commend those words to all hon. members, whether they regard themselves as private enterprisers, socialists, Social Crediters or anything else, because I believe that it is sound advice. There is a point in the economic development of any country in this day and age at which certain forms of industry reach a size and an influence where they begin to affect the daily life of every person in the country; and surely the steel industry, being a basic industry, is becoming one of those industries in Canada.

But to come back to what I was discussing, I was pointing out to the government-unfortunately the Minister of Labour is not in the house at the moment-that one of the solutions is for the steel industry to become a public utility for the use of the Canadian people. As I said before, I am not saying that merely because I want to go on a socializing spree, but for this reason. There seems to be a great deal of conflict in the minds of the hon. members who were on the committee itself, and a great deal more conflict in the minds of other hon. members, as to whether or not the steel companies could actually have paid the increase in wages demanded by the union and still go on making a profit and carrying on with their industry. I have not been able to find figures which could prove that either one way or the other. Neither, apparently, has anyone else, because if we turn to page 131 of the minutes of the committee we find that one hon. member attempted to find out something about the cost of producing steel from Mr. Hilton, and was not given the information. I refer to some questions by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) on page 131. Mr. Hilton had been talking about the rise in the cost of producing steel and the falling off of profits, and so on, and the hon. member said:
Have you a copy of this submission to the wartime prices and trade board?
That was a submission of the steel company to the wartime prices and trade board to show that they required this $5 a ton increase in price. Mr. Hilton replied:
I haven't one here.
The hon. member asked:
Q. Is it available?
A. It is confidential information.
That is the kind of reply that the members of the committee got. It was confidential information, so that they were left in the dark as to whether the company could or could not pay increased wages. The union contends that the company can, and the company contends that it cannot. I am inclined to believe that the union know what they are talking about, because, after all, they are the men who are engaged in the industry; they are the ones who make the production of steel possible. I have as much

confidence in the knowledge of the steel industry by the leaders of the union as I have in the president of the company.
But let me refer to another attempt which was made, in this house, to get that information. On July 11, 1946, a return was brought down in the name of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), in which one of the questions in reference to the costs in the production of steel was this:
3. What is the actual cost of production of a ton of ingot steel in each of the three basic producers' plants?
We turn to the reply, which is this:
It is contrary to the board's policy that financial information of individual concerns, which is obtained in confidence, be released.
How is it going to be possible for the members of the committee or the members of this house to decide whether these companies can pay the increased wages, whether the profits which they say they are making are the correct figures-and Stelco admits making over $4,000,000 of profit last year? We do not know whether these figures are exact. We have no access to their books. We have no way of proving to our own mind and conscience what action we should take in this matter. Therefore I say, if this basic industry were made a public utility the government would be in full possession of all the facts and figures. They could, if they wanted to-and I have no reason to believe that they would not want to-call in the union leadership, show them the books, give the facts, and say, "Here is what we are producing; here is what this industry is earning; here are the wages which we feel we can pay without depriving it of the capital required for expansion; that is the most we can offer you." Then, if the amount the government can offer is still less than is required for a minimum standard of living, I believe the union should apply to the government of this country for a subsidy for that industry in order that it may be able to pay a wage which will give the workers a decent standard of living. The decision which will have to be made in the last analysis is this: do we want production of steel in this country? Is it an industry, a form of production which is basic and necessary to our economy? If it is, we shall have to see to it that steel is produced. If the private concerns who are in charge of it to-day cannot see eye-to-eye with the working man who makes the production possible, and will not under any circumstances let anybody know what the actual cost of production is, because it is confidential information, the only course left is for the government to see to it that that industry is operated in the interests of the people.

If we start from the cold and technical angle that law is the basis of society, regardless of where justice lies, then we shall be in for trouble.
That brings me to the last thing I should like to say, namely, that a great deal has been said in this and other debates about the division of the income of industry, or the productivity of industry, between capital and labour. So far as I am concerned, I say emphatically that I am not satisfied to put labour in the same category as capital. I do not look upon these two things in the same light, because in my mind

and I can go back again to Adam Smith to prove my point if necessary-capital is only an incidental of labour. Labour is the original state

of things. There is only one form of wealth in this or in any country, and that is the wealth produced by applying labour to natural resources. Capital and all the rest of the things incidental to it were created by labour in the first place. But to-day capital has got itself into the position where it has become the golden calf of our economic system. To-day capital puts itself on the pedestal, on the same level as labour and sometimes a little higher, and it says to labour, We shall decide how much of the product of your labour you shall have. I object to that.
We must get back to fundamentals and 'realize that there is only one source of wealth, namely human labour applied1 to natural wealth. The sooner we realize that, the sooner we shall realize that when men go out on strike and ask for the product of their own labour, they are doing it, not because they are communists, but because they are human beings with a sense of righteousness and justice in their hearts for which they are willing to fight.

And so on; which indicates that nearly six weeks ago the government recognized that there was a serious national problem on our hands. A few days later, on July 16, the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) introduced his motion, which called attention to the fact that we had one of the most serious peace-time problems that we had encountered. He said, as reported at page 3488 of Hansard:
The steel strike in Canada must focus the attention of thinking men and women on the broad question of industrial relations. We have had many troubles recently. Some have been settled and some have not.
Then he goes on to make a suggestion. He said:

All who listened to the hon. member for Calgary West felt that he was speaking sincerely in trying to focus the attention of parliament and of the country on this problem.
On August 22, we are dealing with the report of the committee. We have listened to two cabinet ministers who are vitally concerned, the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Labour (Mr.' Mitchell). I submit that the statements made by these two ministers are unsatisfactory to parliament and to the country. I consider that we would be failing to discharge our duties if we accepted the report of the committee and the statement of these two ministers and hurried away to our homes without facing up to this problem. If the problem were as serious as it was said to be on July 16-and it was-then parliament must face up to it and demand that the cabinet should give a statement other than the one we have listened to to-night from the Minister of Labour and the one given by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, some days ago.
Speaking in this debate on August 20, as reported at page 5128 of Hansard, the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply said:
Meantime, while the committee was sitting, strikes in a number of basic industries were in progress. Not only have they paralysed industries directly affected, but they are extending to industries not directly associated with any labour dispute. That situation is most acute at this moment. There is scarcely a section of the country which is not beginning to be affected by these strikes.
Then on the next page the minister concluded:
It gets so had that it is impossible to perpetuate itself. I believe that these strikes are nearing the point when they will either solve themselves or be capable of solution. I believe the work of the committee has contributed toward bringing about that situation, and I can assure the Minister of Labour that anything I can do as Minister of Reconstruction and Supply to assist in bringing these strikes to an early conclusion, will be done.
That is not a useful contribution to make to a debate of this kind, to suggest that possibly the strikers will be starved into surrender and somehow, sometime, the matter will solve itself. If we leave without some indication of what government policy is to be, there will certainly be other strikes. It has been announced that a strike in the meat-packing industry is pending. I think it is fairly obvious that, even although management and labour might be able to get together in the meatpacking industries, even though Canada Packers might agree that they could grant an increase of twelve cents an hour, it would be impossible for such a decision to be reached while government policy is as it is. Certainly no union would be able to convince its mem-

Industrial Relations
bership that if a company can afford only six cents or seven cents, it should accept that sort of compromise. If we leave here and we have strikes in the transportation field, the meatpacking industry and a number of other most essential industries, this country will be faced with one of the most serious peace-time conditions that we have ever known.
I am very sorry the members of the house did not have an opportunity to refer this report back to the committee. I see no good reason why the house could not be adjourned instead of proroguing, as we did during the war on several occasions when it was felt that it might be necessary to call us together to deal with urgent national matters. I see no reason why the committee might not have continued its deliberations. Several of the members of the committee who have spoken have indicated that they worked under tremendous pressure, and that they were not satisfied with the amount of time at their disposal. Others who have taken part in the debate have drawn attention to serious items which were overlooked. The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), a supporter of the government, made a telling criticism of paragraph 6, which reads:

Several hon. members who have participated in the debate suggested that, after parliament adjourns, action might be taken by the government at Stelco in Hamilton, that the decision might be taken by those within the plant that the previous vote had not been taken in a legal way, and the Minister of Labour indicated that he would make the position very clear. I want to point out that the minister and Donald Gordon have taken the stand that a ten-cent increase is all that the price ceiling will allow. It has not been made clear in this debate, nor . was it made clear to the committee, why the ten cents was pulled out of the air. Why was it not nine; why was it not two? Why did you reach ten cents?
The five-cent increase means an additional forty cents a day. I noticed in the evidence the management of Stelco would not come clean and put their cards on the table to demonstrate that they could not pay this increase, or that they could not have carried on if they had not had the $5 a ton increase.
I was in the United States last winter when their steel strike was in progress. The dispute there was not as to whether the steel companies could afford to pay more. They took the position that it was not the business of the unions to know whether or not the extra could be paid. My information was that the steel companies there could close for six months during the present year and be in a better financial position at the end of the year than they were in any ten, years prior to the outbreak of the war. Their plan was to close down and break the unions.
Fortunately the administration in the United States recognized that this course of action could not be followed. They gave the companies an increase of $5 a ton, but it was mandatory that those companies in the United States should pay an additional 18i cents an hour.
I am not surprised that hon. members in the committee were favourably impressed by the labour representatives who gave evidence before the committe,. Those men made it quite clear that they were not asking for anything that would put the steel companies out of business. I am sure all members of parliament were interested in the little booklet that was presented to them, to give us information regarding the situation. This was given weeks before the strike broke out, and it pointed out that unless something was done, a strike would take place.
Industrial Relations

A number of questions were asked and discussed frankly. Is 833.60 a week too much? The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) posed that question this morning. No member of parliament has risen in his place and said that $33.60 a week, or $1,750 a year, is too much in this day and age.
We have come to the end of the war which has enabled us to do many spectacular things in the field of production. We contributed generously to mutual aid. We managed to maintain a measure of price control, which, I agree, was more satisfactory than they had in the United States. It was very satisfactory, considering all the factors concerned.
But I admit that Donald Gordon is unreasonable when he takes the position that the Canadian economy will not permit $33.60 a week for these steel workers. Just this week we passed a bill giving increased salaries to judges. According to the public accounts, I find that 271 judges are to have an increase of $637,000 in the next year. I admit that brings a lot of pressure on the price ceiling. Yet Donald Gordon did not raise his voice in protest.
As the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) said:, it is all right to give $20,000 to a judge who is already getting $15,000, or to give $16,000 to one who is now getting $12,000, but it is not all right to give this increase to the steel workers! I understand that the increase the steel workers are seeking would cost Stelco an additional $2,500,000. "$2,500,000 more for the steel workers?-we cannot do it." But, "$670,000 for the judges? -why, that is no problem at all."
Hon. members last year participated in legislation to increase our "take-home pay." I supported it, and1 I take my share of responsibility for it. But I must not lose sight of the fact that what I have done for myself I should do for the other fellow. Two hundred and forty-five members and ninety-six senators voted themselves an additional $2,000 a year, or a total of $682,000 for 341 parliamentarians, and yet Donald Gordon said that we could not give the steel workers in the steel companies an additional $2,500,000 in order to bring their minimum wage up to $33 a week, or $1,750 a year.

At this point the "practical man" enters. He says: "All this is very fine. No one wants to see steel workers getting less than $33.60 a week. Industrial Relations
You see, despite all the talk you hear about workers and employers being "partners'' or members of "one big, happy family," the working partners in the steel industry don't know for certain what the owning partners really earn. The owners don't give their employees that confidential information. It seems as if the best the steel workers can ever get is the flat assurance that, whatever their request might be, the company can't afford it. Peculiarly enough, after an increase is granted, the company does manage to keep on going.
However, on the basis of what can be found out from study of public financial reports, here is what seems to be the case.
Take the three big steel companies, for example.
They all functioned during the war and didn't lose any money. They show increases in profits and peculiar increases in reserves, capital value, depreciation reserves, etc. All of them received support, in cash, buildings and equipment from the government.

I find I am in essential agreement with the hon. member for Calgary West. In connection with the ten-cent ceiling I want to say that I think it has been pretty well established by now that if the fifteen-cent increase had been granted the pressure on the price ceiling would not have been nearly as great as has been created by the prolonged strikes. I cannot prove this, but I have been advised that nails are selling in several parts of Canada at $25 per 100 pounds. I am sure that if this strike continues, the serious shortage of supplies will create a much greater pressure on the price ceiling and make it more difficult to maintain controls than if a reasonable increase had been granted.
To come back to these companies, when Donald Gordon was before the committee he pointed out the difficulty they had had in getting financial statements from the steel companies when pressure was being brought to bear to grant a $5 per ton increase. He said: We laid down the position that we would have to be shown that their over-all position was such that they would be in a poor financial condition. Mr. McMaster took violent objection to that.
And again:
I should say to the committee that we leaned heavily upon the company for the factual infqr-mation we required, and while we tested that information to the best of our ability, it is true that we depended largely upon the accuracy of the steel company's figures.
The hon. member for Cariboo made it quite clear that that sort of evidence was not satisfactory. Last night, when the leader of this party was speaking, the Minister of Labour interjected to say that their traditions were such that they did not run away from problems. While it is getting late in the season and many members have made commitments that are pressing, I feel we would be failing in our responsibility to the Canadian people if we left for home without having some formula from the administration that would indicate what will happen in the industries now on strike and in the other industries that are going on strike.

Mr. Speaker, the subject of industrial relations has been pretty well covered. I do not intend to bring up any new points this evening, but I want to go on record with respect to one thing. I agree with the members who have urged that this house should remain in session until this strike has been settled. I am not going to say any more on that.
I was a member of the industrial relations committee, but unfortunately I was called back home and had to resign from the committee. Every member of the committee did

Industrial Relations
his best to find a solution of this problem. The evidence given by one man stands out in the industrial relations committee. That was the evidence given by Mr. Donald Gordon of the wartime prices and trade board. Apparently the members of the committee were unable to break down the statement made by Mr. Gordon that a ten-cent increase in wages to the steel workers would break the price ceiling structure in this country. When that point was made I think the committee and the government should have got together to get all the facts with respect to the situation and either break down that argument or admit that it was sound. Personally I do not think it is sound.
